question: Were both the Battle of Stones River and the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River fought in the 19th century?
context:
[d06p000] Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River
[d06s000] The Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River, also known as the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on () or the Second Phase Campaign Western Sector (), was a decisive battle in the Korean War, and it took place from November 25 to December 2, 1950, along the Ch'ongch'on River Valley in the northwestern part of North Korea.
[d06s001] In response to the successful Chinese First Phase Campaign against the United Nations forces, General Douglas MacArthur launched the Home-by-Christmas Offensive to evict the Chinese forces from Korea and to end the war.
[d06s002] Anticipating this reaction, the Chinese People's Volunteer Army Commander Peng Dehuai planned a counteroffensive, dubbed the "Second Phase Campaign", against the advancing UN forces.

[d04p000] Battle of Stones River
[d04s000] The Battle of Stones River or Second Battle of Murfreesboro, was fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863, in Middle Tennessee, as the culmination of the Stones River Campaign in the Western Theater of the American Civil War.
[d04s001] Of the major battles of the Civil War, Stones River had the highest percentage of casualties on both sides.
[d04s002] Although the battle itself was inconclusive, the Union Army's repulse of two Confederate attacks and the subsequent Confederate withdrawal were a much-needed boost to Union morale after the defeat at the Battle of Fredericksburg, and it dashed Confederate aspirations for control of Middle Tennessee.

[d03p003] Umba River (Tanzania)
[d03s003] Just before the Umba flows into the Indian Ocean, it crosses the border to Kenya.
[d03s004] The mouth itself marks the most eastern point on the border between Tanzania and Kenya, which was largely made in a straight line to the northwest towards Lake Victoria in the 19th Century.
[d03s005] On the upper reaches of the river in the mid-1960s rich deposits of precious stones, including sapphires and Spessartine, were discovered.

[d08p003] Collins Ferry Historic District
[d08s003] The Collins Farm includes 19th century farm outbuildings, the family cemetery, a mill site along the river, and the site where stones for the mill's construction and grinding stones were quarried.
[d08s004] The Hubbard Farm is located south and east of the Collins Farm, and is accessed via a private drive that forms part of the historic road leading to Collins Ferry.
[d08s005] Hubbard Farm includes a Greek Revival farmhouse built in 1856, and also includes 19th century outbuildings, a family cemetery, and the remains of a slave quarters.

[d00p000] Battle of Glendale (Skye)
[d00s000] The Battle of Glendale was a battle fought on the Inner Hebridean island of Skye, between the MacDonalds of Sleat and the MacDonalds of Clanranald, against the MacLeods of Harris and Dunvegan and the MacLeods of Lewis.
[d00s001] According to MacLeod tradition preserved in the early 19th century, the battle was fought in about the year 1490; yet it has been recently suggested that the battle more likely took place sometime after 1513.
[d00s002] MacLeod tradition records that the battle was the 'most tremendous battle' that the clan ever fought—although the clan was victorious, it never fully recovered from its severe losses.

[d05p000] Joseph L. Follett
[d05s000] Joseph Leonard Follett (February 16, 1843 – April 1, 1907) was an American soldier who fought in the American Civil War.
[d05s001] Follett received the country's highest award for bravery during combat, the Medal of Honor, for his action during the Battle of Island Number Ten in New Madrid, Missouri on 3 March 1862 and the Battle of Stones River in Tennessee on 31 December 1862.
[d05s002] He was honored with the award on 19 September 1890.

[d02p000] Register Cliff
[d02s000] Register Cliff is a sandstone cliff and featured key navigational landmark prominently listed in the 19th century guidebooks about the Oregon Trail, and a place where many emigrants chiseled the names of their families on the soft stones of the cliff it was one of the key checkpoint landmarks for parties heading west along the Platte River valley west of Fort John, Wyoming which allowed travelers to verify they were on the correct path up to South Pass and not moving into impassable mountain terrainsgeographically, it is on the eastern ascent of the Continental divide leading upward out of the great plains in the east of the U.S. state of Wyoming.
[d02s001] It is notable as a historic landmark for 'registering' hundreds of emigrants on the Oregon Trail (thus also the other northern Emigrant Trails that split off farther west such as the California Trail and Mormon Trail) who came to follow custom and inscribed their names on its rocks during the western migrations of the 19th century.
[d02s002] An estimated 500,000 emigrants used these trails from 1843–1869, with up to one-tenth dying along the way, usually due to disease.

[d01p000] Battle of Berestechko
[d01s000] The Battle of Berestechko (Polish: "Bitwa pod Beresteczkiem" ; Ukrainian: Берестецька битва, Битва під Берестечком ) was fought between the Ukrainian Cossacks, led by Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky, aided by their Crimean Tatar allies, and a Polish army under King John II Casimir.
[d01s001] It was a battle of a Cossack rebellion in Ukraine that took place in the years 1648–1657 after the expiration of a two-year truce.
[d01s002] Fought from 28 to 30 June 1651, the battle took place in the province of Volhynia, on the hilly plain south of the Styr River.

After the Spanish conquest of Mexico in the 16th century, indigenous tribes were defeated by Spain, thus beginning a three century era of Spanish dominance.

question: Cinnamon sugar is a spice used to flavor this traditional Spanish and Portugese fried pastry.
context:
[d01p000] Cinnamon sugar
[d01s000] Cinnamon sugar is a mixture of ground cinnamon and granulated sugar used as a spice for desserts.
[d01s001] It is commonly used to flavor foods such as Belgian waffles, Snickerdoodle cookies, churros and coffee cake.
[d01s002] It is also found in breakfast cereals such as Cinnamon Toast Crunch.

[d02p000] Mixed spice
[d02s000] Mixed spice, also called pudding spice, is a British blend of sweet spices, similar to the pumpkin pie spice used in the United States.
[d02s001] Cinnamon is the dominant flavour, with nutmeg and allspice.
[d02s002] It is often used in baking, or to complement fruits or other sweet foods.

[d04p000] Sopaipilla
[d04s000] A sopaipilla, sopapilla, sopaipa, or cachanga is a kind of fried pastry and a type of quick bread served in several regions with Spanish heritage in the Americas.
[d04s001] The word sopaipilla is the diminutive of sopaipa, a word that entered Spanish from the Mozarabic language of Al-Andalus.
[d04s002] The original Mozarabic word "Xopaipa" was used to mean bread soaked in oil, and derived in turn from the Germanic word "suppa" which meant bread soaked in liquid.

[d07p000] Churro
[d07s000] A churro (] , ] ) is a fried-dough pastry—predominantly choux—based snack.
[d07s001] Churros are traditional in Spain and Portugal - from where they originate - as well as the Philippines and Ibero-America.
[d07s002] They are also consumed in the Southwestern United States, France and other areas that have received immigration from Spanish and Portuguese-speaking countries.

[d08p000] Cinnamon leaf oil
[d08s000] Cinnamon leaf oil is obtained by steam distillation of cinnamon leaves and the oil yield ranges between 0.5% and 1.8%.
[d08s001] More than 47 compounds have been identified from the leaf oil, the most significant being eugenol, which constitutes 65–92% .
[d08s002] Cinnamon leaf oil is cheaper than bark oil and is used in the flavor industry, to a lesser extent, to flavor confectionary.

[d06p003] Cinnamon roll
[d06s003] Its main ingredients are flour, cinnamon, sugar, and butter, which provide a robust and sweet flavor.
[d06s004] In some places, it is eaten as a breakfast food and is served with cream cheese or icing.

[d08p003] Cinnamon leaf oil
[d08s003] It is also used as a source of eugenol for the preparation of synthetic vanillin.
[d08s004] Cinnamon oleoresin obtained by solvent extraction is a dark brown extremely concentrated and viscous liquid, closely approximating the total spice flavour and containing 50% or more volatile oil.
[d08s005] It is used mainly for flavouring food products such as cakes and confectionary.

[d03p000] Cruller
[d03s000] A traditional cruller (or twister) is a fried pastry often made from a rectangle of dough, with a cut made in the middle that allows it to be pulled over and through itself producing twists in the sides of the pastry.
[d03s001] Crullers have been described as resembling "a small, braided torpedo" and having been "a staple of the New England diet since the Pilgrims' day".
[d03s002] Some other cruller styles are made of a denser dough somewhat like that of a cake doughnut formed in a small loaf or stick shape, but not always twisted.

[d05p000] Nuegados
[d05s000] Nuegados is a traditional plate from many different countries in Latin America.
[d05s001] However, it is only in "El Salvador that they are called 'nuégados'" (Latinaish, Salvadoran Nuegados) Nuegados are "nothing more than fried dumplings coated with a sweet sugar cane sauce".
[d05s002] To prepare nuegados, one deep fries a dough made of corn flour, baking powder, butter, salt, and water in oil.

[d03p003] Cruller
[d03s003] Crullers may be topped with plain powdered sugar; powdered sugar mixed with cinnamon; or icing.
[d03s004] However, a "French cruller" is a fluted, ring-shaped doughnut made from choux pastry with a light airy texture.
[d03s005] The French cruller in German is called a Spritzkuchen.

question: Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 139) hosted an event by what organization on Oct 12, 1991?
context:
[d07p000] 1991 Ms. Olympia
[d07s000] The 1991 Ms. Olympia contest was an IFBB professional bodybuilding competition was held on October 12 and 13, 1991 at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles, California.
[d07s001] It was the 12th Ms. Olympia competition held.

[d05p000] Shrine Auditorium
[d05s000] The Shrine Auditorium is a landmark large-event venue in Los Angeles, California.
[d05s001] It is also the headquarters of the Al Malaikah Temple, a division of the Shriners.
[d05s002] It was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 139) in 1975.

[d00p000] Birthplace of Adlai E. Stevenson II
[d00s000] Birthplace of Adlai E. Stevenson II is a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 35) in the West Adams neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d00s001] The site was the birthplace of two-time US Presidential candidate Adlai E. Stevenson II, who was born there on February 5, 1900.
[d00s002] The house was designed by C.W. Wedgewood and built in approximately 1894.

[d03p000] Forthmann Carriage House
[d03s000] The Forthmann Carriage House, is a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 103) located in Angelino Heights, Los Angeles, California.
[d03s001] It is a 1,000 sq. ft. Victorian style carriage house built 1882, designed by Burgess J. Reeve.
[d03s002] It was relocated in March 2006 from its original location at 629 West 18th Street.

[d01p003] Elkay Apartments
[d01s003] The building is owned today by his daughter Karen Bruderlin It is next door to the Kelton Apartments designed by Neutra in 1941 for himself.
[d01s004] Despite objections from the owners of the Elkay Apartments, on June 21, 1988, the City of Los Angeles designated the building a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument.

[d09p003] Susana Machado Bernard House and Barn
[d09s003] Noted for its Gothic style with soaring spaces, the house has vaulted ceilings and curved walls.
[d09s004] In 1979, it was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (HCM #208), and listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
[d09s005] The property was purchased in 1996 by the Center for Human Rights & Constitutional Law.

[d08p000] The Barry Building
[d08s000] The Barry Building is a landmark commercial mid-twentieth century modern building located at 11973 San Vicente Boulevard in the heart of the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d08s001] It was designed by architect Milton Caughey (1911-1958) and completed in 1951.
[d08s002] In 2007, the building was listed as a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument,(Historical Cultural Monument #887), making it one of the few mid-century modern commercial buildings to gain such status.

[d06p009] Powder Magazine (Camp Drum)
[d06s009] When the larger structure was torn down, the Powder Magazine was re-discovered.
[d06s010] In order to save it from demolition, it was declared a Historic-Cultural Monument (HCM #249) in August 1982.
[d06s011] For more than two decades, it has sat on a vacant, fenced-off lot two blocks south of the Drum Barracks.

[d02p000] Millennium Biltmore Hotel
[d02s000] The Millennium Biltmore Hotel, originally named the Los Angeles Biltmore Hotel of the Biltmore Hotels group, is a luxury hotel located across the street from Pershing Square in Downtown Los Angeles, California, US.
[d02s001] Upon its grand opening in 1923, the Los Angeles Biltmore was the largest hotel west of Chicago, Illinois in the United States.
[d02s002] In 1969 the Biltmore Hotel was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument by the City of Los Angeles.

[d01p000] Elkay Apartments
[d01s000] The Elkay Apartments is an historic five-unit two-story multi-family building located at 638-642 Kelton Avenue, in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d01s001] Designed in 1948 in the international or modernistic style of architecture by noted Los Angeles architect Richard Neutra, it was completed in 1948 for noted violist Louis Kievman.
[d01s002] The name Elkay is derived from his initials.

[d06s001] It is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films of the franchise, and was produced by ABC Studios, Marvel Television, and F&B Fazekas & Butters.

question: Which opera has more acts, Parsifal or Manon by Massenet?
context:
[d00p000] Parsifal
[d00s000] Parsifal (WWV 111) is an opera in three acts by German composer Richard Wagner.
[d00s001] It is loosely based on "Parzival" by Wolfram von Eschenbach, a 13th-century epic poem of the Arthurian knight Parzival (Percival) and his quest for the Holy Grail (12th century).

[d06p000] Manon Lescaut (Auber)
[d06s000] Manon Lescaut is an opera or opéra comique in 3 acts by Daniel Auber to a libretto by Eugène Scribe, and, like Puccini's "Manon Lescaut" and Massenet's "Manon", is based on the Abbé Prévost's novel "Manon Lescaut".
[d06s001] Auber's version is nowadays the least-performed of the three.

[d08p003] Jean-Claude Auvray
[d08s003] Among his 150 and more productions are "Tancredi" (Rossini), "La Gioconda" (Ponchielli), "Tristan und Isolde" (Wagner), "Manon" (Massenet), "Peter Grimes" (Britten), "Fidelio" (Beethoven), "Otello, "Aida" (Verdi), "La bohème" and "Gianni Schicchi" (Puccini).
[d08s004] Between 1996 and 2006 he directed plays at the Israeli Opera.

[d04p000] Renée Fleming
[d04s000] Renée Fleming (born February 14, 1959) is an American opera singer and soprano whose repertoire encompasses Richard Strauss, Mozart, Handel, bel canto, lieder, French opera and chansons, jazz and indie rock.
[d04s001] Fleming has a full lyric soprano voice.
[d04s002] She has performed coloratura, lyric, and lighter spinto soprano operatic roles in Italian, German, French, Czech, and Russian, aside from her native English.

[d01p000] Manon Lescaut (Puccini)
[d01s000] Manon Lescaut is an opera in four acts by Giacomo Puccini, composed between 1890 and 1893.
[d01s001] The story is based on the 1731 novel "L'histoire du chevalier des Grieux et de Manon Lescaut" by the Abbé Prévost and should not be confused with "Manon", an 1884 opera by Jules Massenet based on the same novel.

[d03p000] Boulevard Solitude
[d03s000] Boulevard Solitude is a "Lyrisches Drama " (lyric drama) or opera in one act by Hans Werner Henze to a German libretto by Grete Weil after the play by Walter Jockisch, in its turn a modern retelling of François Prévost's "Manon Lescaut".
[d03s001] The piece is a reworking of the Manon Lescaut story, already adapted operatically by Auber, Massenet and Puccini, and here relocated to Paris after the Second World War where, as is noted in Grove, the focus of the story moves away from Manon and towards Armand des Grieux.
[d03s002] It became Henze’s first fully-fledged opera.

[d07p000] Manon
[d07s000] Manon (] ) is an "opéra comique" in five acts by Jules Massenet to a French libretto by Henri Meilhac and Philippe Gille, based on the 1731 novel "L’histoire du chevalier des Grieux et de Manon Lescaut" by the Abbé Prévost.
[d07s001] It was first performed at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 19 January 1884, with sets designed by Eugène Carpezat (Act I), Auguste-Alfred Rubé and Philippe Chaperon (Acts II and III), and Jean-Baptiste Lavastre (Act IV).

[d02p000] Manon (disambiguation)
[d02s000] Manon is an opera by Jules Massenet, adapted from Abbé Prévost's novel "Manon Lescaut".

[d09p000] L'histoire de Manon
[d09s000] L'histoire de Manon, generally referred to as "Manon", is a ballet choreographed by Kenneth MacMillan to music by Jules Massenet and based on the 1731 novel "Manon Lescaut" by Abbé Prévost.
[d09s001] The ballet was first performed by The Royal Ballet in London in 1974 with Antoinette Sibley and Anthony Dowell in the leading roles.
[d09s002] It continues to be performed and recognised internationally.

[d05p000] Massenet Festival
[d05s000] Massenet Festival ("Festival Massenet") is a biennale festival of music by French composer, Jules Massenet held in Saint-Étienne, France, close to the area where the composer was born.
[d05s001] The first Massenet Festival took place in November 1990 when the opera "Cléopâtre" and the oratorio "La Vierge" were presented.
[d05s002] In recent years, performances have been given in the Grand Théâtre Massenet, one of the theatres of the Opéra Théâtre de Saint-Etienne, and formerly known as L'Esplanade.

question: Which acter/director is known for depicting the Russian working class life and directed a film that won an Academy Award in 1981?
context:
[d02p003] Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears
[d02s003] The leading roles were played by Vera Alentova and by Aleksey Batalov.
[d02s004] The film won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 1981.

[d00p003] Vladimir Menshov
[d00s003] Although his output as an actor outnumbers his output as a director, he is best known for the five films he directed, the most famous of which is the 1979 melodrama "Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears", which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
[d00s004] Actress Vera Alentova, who starred in the film, is the mother of Vladimir Menshov's daughter Yuliya Menshova.

[d02p000] Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears
[d02s000] Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears (Russian: Москва слезам не верит ; translit.
[d02s001] "Moskva slezam ne verit") is a 1980 Soviet film made by Mosfilm.
[d02s002] It was written by Valentin Chernykh and directed by Vladimir Menshov.

[d06p000] Letter to Brezhnev
[d06s000] Letter to Brezhnev is a 1985 British romantic comedy film about working class life in contemporary Liverpool.
[d06s001] It was written by Frank Clarke and directed by Chris Bernard.
[d06s002] It starred Alexandra Pigg, Margi Clarke, Alfred Molina, Peter Firth and Tracy Marshak-Nash (credited as Tracy Lea).

[d00p000] Vladimir Menshov
[d00s000] Vladimir Valentinovich Menshov (Russian: Влади́мир Валенти́нович Меньшо́в ; born 17 September 1939 in Baku) is a Soviet and Russian actor and film director.
[d00s001] He is noted for depicting the Russian everyman and working class life in his films.
[d00s002] Like many other Russian filmmakers, he studied acting and directing at the state film school VGIK, the world's oldest educational institution in cinematography.

[d09p000] Stanley Aronowitz
[d09s000] Stanley Aronowitz (born January 6, 1933) is a professor of sociology, cultural studies, and urban education at the CUNY Graduate Center.
[d09s001] He is also a veteran political activist and cultural critic, an advocate for organized labor and a member of the interim consultative committee of the International Organization for a Participatory Society.
[d09s002] In 2012, Aronowitz was awarded the Center for Study of Working Class Life's Lifetime Achievement Award at Stony Brook University.

[d01p009] Mario Suárez (writer)
[d01s009] Many of his sketches of immigrant and working class life were published in the mid- to late-1950s.
[d01s010] From an anthropological standpoint, his work should be heralded for telling the immigrant story and documenting life in El Hoyo before its demise.

[d06p003] Letter to Brezhnev
[d06s003] "Letter To Brezhnev" presents Margaret Thatcher's high-unemployment Liverpool as a dangerous and near hopeless city.

[d03p000] Richard Cameron (writer)
[d03s000] Richard Cameron is an English playwright from Doncaster (born (1948--)16 1948 ).
[d03s001] His themes are Northern post-industrial society, working class life, tough women and violent men.
[d03s002] Cameron's plays include "Pond Life" (1992), "Not Fade Away" (1993), "The Mortal Ash" (1994), "All of You Mine" (1996), "The Glee Club" (2002), "Gong Donkeys" (2004), "Flower Girls" (2007), and "Can't Stand Up For Falling Down".

[d08p000] Louis Guilloux
[d08s000] Louis Guilloux (15 January 1899 – 14 October 1980) was a French writer born in Saint-Brieuc, Brittany, where he lived throughout his life.
[d08s001] He is known for his Social Realist novels describing working class life and political struggles in the mid-twentieth century.
[d08s002] His best-known book is "Le Sang noir" (Blood Dark), which has been described as a "prefiguration of Sartre's "La Nausée"."

[d06s000] Johannes, Jan or Johan Vermeer ( ; ] ; October 1632 – December 1675) was a Dutch painter who specialized in domestic interior scenes of middle-class life.
[d06s001] Vermeer was a moderately successful provincial genre painter in his lifetime.
[d06s002] He evidently was not wealthy, leaving his wife and children in debt at his death, perhaps because he produced relatively few paintings.

[d01p000] The Lacemaker (Vermeer)
[d01s000] The Lacemaker is a painting by the Dutch artist Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675), completed around 1669–1670 and held in the Louvre, Paris.
[d01s001] The work shows a young woman dressed in a yellow shawl, holding up a pair of bobbins in her left hand as she carefully places a pin in the pillow on which she is making her bobbin lace.
[d01s002] At 24.5 cm x 21 cm (9.6 in x 8.3 in), the work is the smallest of Vermeer's paintings, but in many ways one of his most abstract and unusual.

[d00s001] He specialized in landscapes, farms and interior scenes, with figures, and was one of the first Pointillist painters in the Netherlands.

[d02p000] Pieter Janssens Elinga
[d02s000] Pieter Janssens Elinga (1623–1682) was a Dutch Golden Age painter, mainly of domestic interior scenes with a strong emphasis on the rectangular geometrical elements of windows, floor tiling paintings, and other elements, and a few genre figures.

[d03s001] He studied under Nicolas Gosse and was a pupil of Antoine-Jean Gros.
[d03s002] He entered the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris in 1817 and exhibited his work at the Salon (Paris) between 1831 and 1843.

[d07p000] Annunciation (Memling)

[d07s001] Completed c. 1482, it was partially transferred to canvas in the 1920s and is today held in the Robert Lehman collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
[d07s002] It shows the Virgin in a domestic interior, two attendant angels, the archangel Gabriel dressed in rich ecclesiastical robes, and a hovering dove.

[d06p000] Atatürk Museum Mansion

[d08s000] The Atatürk Museum in Mersin (Turkish: "Mersin Atatürk Evi Müzesi" ) is a two-storey house in Mersin, which hosted the founder of modern Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and his wife in 1925.

[d00s001] Founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, a Turkish army officer, revolutionary, and the first President of Turkey, the Izmir Atatürk Museum opened to the public on 11 September 1941, on the 19th anniversary of Atatürk’s arrival in Izmir.

[d07s003] He was first in his class under Vedat Tek in 1928, and later worked with Hans Poelzig in Germany.
[d07s004] In 193 he designed the Glass Villa of Çankaya Köşkü, the President of Turkey's official residence, as well as Florya Atatürk Marine Mansion, a Bauhaus-style former residence of Atatürk and now a museum, in 1935.

question: What ABC television series was inspired by a 2011 film and cast Dominic Cooper as young Howard Stark?

[d09s000] Dominic Edward Cooper (born 2 June 1978) is an English actor.

[d09s002] " and as the young Howard Stark in the Marvel Cinematic Universe including "" and "Agent Carter".

[d01p000] Agent Carter (TV series)
[d01s000] Marvel's Agent Carter, or simply Agent Carter, is an American television series created for ABC by Christopher Markus & Stephen McFeely, inspired by the 2011 film "", and the 2013 Marvel One-Shot short film of the same name.
[d01s001] It is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films and other television series of the franchise.
[d01s002] The series was produced by ABC Studios, Marvel Television, and F&B Fazekas & Butters, with Tara Butters, Michele Fazekas, and Chris Dingess serving as showrunners.

[d08p000] Preacher (TV series)
[d08s000] Preacher is an American television series developed by Sam Catlin, Evan Goldberg, and Seth Rogen for AMC starring Dominic Cooper.
[d08s001] It is an adaptation of the comic book series "Preacher" created by Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon, and published by DC Comics' Vertigo imprint.
[d08s002] The series was officially picked up on September 9, 2015, with a ten-episode order which premiered on May 22, 2016.

[d09p003] Dominic Cooper
[d09s003] He stars as Jesse Custer on the AMC show "Preacher" (2016–present).

[d07p000] James D'Arcy
[d07s000] James D'Arcy (born Simon Richard D'Arcy; 24 August 1975) is an English actor.
[d07s001] He is best known for his portrayals of Howard Stark's butler, Edwin Jarvis, in the Marvel Entertainment and ABC series, "Agent Carter", and murder suspect Lee Ashworth in the second series of the ITV series "Broadchurch".
[d07s002] D'Arcy also co-starred as a British Army Colonel in Christopher Nolan's action-thriller "Dunkirk" (2017).

[d03p000] John Slattery
[d03s000] John M. Slattery Jr. (born August 13, 1962) is an American actor and director.
[d03s001] He is best known for his role as Roger Sterling in the AMC drama series "Mad Men" and for his role as Howard Stark in cameo appearances in the Marvel Cinematic Universe films "Iron Man 2", "Ant-Man", and "".
[d03s002] He has received four Primetime Emmy Awards nominations and two Critics' Choice Television Awards for "Mad Men".

[d00p000] Now is Not the End
[d00s000] "Now is Not the End" is the first episode of the first season of the American television series "Agent Carter", inspired by the films "" and "", and the Marvel One-Shot short film also titled "Agent Carter".
[d00s001] It features the Marvel Comics character Peggy Carter as she goes undercover to try and clear the name of her friend Howard Stark, and is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films of the franchise.
[d00s002] The episode was written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely and directed by Louis D'Esposito.

[d05p000] Stratton (film)
[d05s000] Stratton is a British action thriller film directed by Simon West, based on the novel series of same name by Duncan Falconer.
[d05s001] The series' lead character John Stratton is played by Dominic Cooper, while the rest of the cast includes Gemma Chan, Austin Stowell, Tyler Hoechlin, and Tom Felton.
[d05s002] Principal photography on the film began on 15 July 2015 in Brindisi, Italy.

[d06p000] Agent Carter (season 1)
[d06s000] The first season of the American television series "Agent Carter", which is inspired by the film "" and the Marvel One-Shot short film of the same name, features the Marvel Comics character Peggy Carter as she must balance doing administrative work and going on secret missions for Howard Stark while trying to navigate life as a single woman in 1940s America.
[d06s001] It is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films of the franchise, and was produced by ABC Studios, Marvel Television, and F&B Fazekas & Butters.
[d06s002] Tara Butters, Michele Fazekas, and Chris Dingess served as showrunners.

[d04p000] The Blitzkrieg Button
[d04s000] "The Blitzkrieg Button" is the fourth episode of the first season of the American television series "Agent Carter", inspired by the films "" and "", and the Marvel One-Shot short film also titled "Agent Carter".
[d04s001] It features the Marvel Comics character Peggy Carter as she must hide the fugitive Howard Stark while she retrieves the titular device for him, and is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films of the franchise.
[d04s002] The episode was written by Brant Englestein and directed by Stephen Cragg.

question: Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria that stretches from Stonethwaite which is a part of a valley and civil parrish in what Borough?
context:
[d06p000] Glaramara
[d06s000] Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria.
[d06s001] It is a substantial fell that is part of a long ridge that stretches for over six kilometres from Stonethwaite in Borrowdale up to the important mountain pass of Esk Hause.
[d06s002] The summit of Glaramara at 783 m (2,569 ft) is the central point of this ridge, which separates the valleys of Langstrath and Grains Gill.

[d04p000] Stonethwaite
[d04s000] Stonethwaite is a small village in the Lake District in the English county of Cumbria.
[d04s001] Historically part of Cumberland, it is situated in the valley of the Stonethwaite Beck, a side valley of Borrowdale, and within the Lake District National Park.
[d04s002] It is on the Cumbria Way long distance footpath.

[d01p000] Borrowdale
[d01s000] Borrowdale is a valley and civil parish in the English Lake District in the Borough of Allerdale in Cumbria, England.

[d09p000] Eagle Crag

[d09s001] Impressive walls of crag look down upon Stonethwaite, making Eagle Crag the most arresting sight from that settlement.
[d09s002] It can be climbed direct by the average walker, picking a route between the rock faces.

question: Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria that stretches from Stonethwaite which is a part of a valley and civil parrish in what Borough?
context:
[d06p000] Glaramara
[d06s000] Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria.
[d06s001] It is a substantial fell that is part of a long ridge that stretches for over six kilometres from Stonethwaite in Borrowdale up to the important mountain pass of Esk Hause.
[d06s002] The summit of Glaramara at 783 m (2,569 ft) is the central point of this ridge, which separates the valleys of Langstrath and Grains Gill.

[d04p000] Stonethwaite
[d04s000] Stonethwaite is a small village in the Lake District in the English county of Cumbria.
[d04s001] Historically part of Cumberland, it is situated in the valley of the Stonethwaite Beck, a side valley of Borrowdale, and within the Lake District National Park.
[d04s002] It is on the Cumbria Way long distance footpath.

[d01p000] Borrowdale
[d01s000] Borrowdale is a valley and civil parish in the English Lake District in the Borough of Allerdale in Cumbria, England.

[d09p000] Eagle Crag
[d09s000] Eagle Crag is a fell in the Lake District in Cumbria, England, it is situated near the village of Stonethwaite where the valleys of Langstrath and Greenup join.
[d09s001] Impressive walls of crag look down upon Stonethwaite, making Eagle Crag the most arresting sight from that settlement.
[d09s002] It can be climbed direct by the average walker, picking a route between the rock faces.

[d03p000] Great Crag
[d03s000] Great Crag is a fell in the English Lake District, located near the hamlets of Rosthwaite and Stonethwaite in Borrowdale.

[d08p000] Bowfell
[d08s000] Bowfell (named "Bow Fell" on Ordnance Survey maps) is a pyramid-shaped mountain lying at the heart of the English Lake District, in the Southern Fells area.
[d08s001] It is the sixth-highest mountain in the Lake District and one of the most popular of the Lake District fells for walkers.
[d08s002] It is listed in Alfred Wainwright's 'best half dozen' Lake District fells.

[d00p000] Ritson's Force
[d00s000] Ritson's Force is a set of waterfalls in the valley of Mosedale in the English Lake District.
[d00s001] It is also the river that leads past the Wasdale Head Inn and the Great Gable Brewing Company.
[d00s002] The hills nearby include Sca Fell and Scafell Pike, England's two highest mountains, and Great Gable, home to British climbing.

[d02p000] Blindcrake
[d02s000] Blindcrake is a village and civil parish within the Isel Valley, in the Lake District National Park and in the Allerdale district of Cumbria, England.
[d02s001] According to the 2001 census it had a population of 287, increasing to 348 at the 2011 Census.
[d02s002] The parish includes Blindcrake village and the hamlets of Redmain, Isel and Sunderland, The whole parish lies within the Lake District National Park and, since 2001, Blindcrake village  is one of 23 designated conservation areas of the National Park Planning Authority.

[d05p000] Dock Tarn
[d05s000] Dock Tarn is a small tarn located within the Lake District National Park in Cumbria, England at grid reference [ NY273143] .
[d05s001] It is situated on moorland at 400 metres above sea level near the summit of Great Crag, midway between Watendlath, the Stonethwaite valley and Borrowdale.
[d05s002] It measures approximately 300 by 200 metres, and the shoreline is indented with rocky headlands and bays.

[d02p003] Blindcrake
[d02s003] This status is largely based on its mediaeval strip field pattern which is described as "undoubtedly the finest example of its type in the Lake District".
[d02s004] The parish boundary is approximately defined by the Lake District National Park boundary in the north and west, by a line 2 km to the west of the A591 in the east and by the River Derwent in the south.
[d02s005] It is one of the smallest parishes within the Allerdale district of Cumbria.

[d01s000] Marvel's Agent Carter, or simply Agent Carter, is an American television series created for ABC by Christopher Markus & Stephen McFeely, inspired by the 2011 film "", and the 2013 Marvel One-Shot short film of the same name.
[d01s001] It is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films and other television series of the franchise.

[d06p000] Agent Carter (season 1)
[d06s000] The first season of the American television series "Agent Carter", which is inspired by the film "" and the Marvel One-Shot short film of the same name, features the Marvel Comics character Peggy Carter as she must balance doing administrative work and going on secret missions for Howard Stark while trying to navigate life as a single woman in 1940s America.
[d06s001] It is set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), sharing continuity with the films of the franchise, and was produced by ABC Studios, Marvel Television, and F&B Fazekas & Butters.
[d06s002] Tara Butters, Michele Fazekas, and Chris Dingess served as showrunners.

[d05s000] Stratton is a British action thriller film directed by Simon West, based on the novel series of same name by Duncan Falconer.
[d05s001] The series' lead character John Stratton is played by Dominic Cooper, while the rest of the cast includes Gemma Chan, Austin Stowell, Tyler Hoechlin, and Tom Felton.
[d05s002] Principal photography on the film began on 15 July 2015 in Brindisi, Italy.

[d08p000] Preacher (TV series)
[d08s000] Preacher is an American television series developed by Sam Catlin, Evan Goldberg, and Seth Rogen for AMC starring Dominic Cooper.
[d08s001] It is an adaptation of the comic book series "Preacher" created by Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon, and published by DC Comics' Vertigo imprint.
[d08s002] The series was officially picked up on September 9, 2015, with a ten-episode order which premiered on May 22, 2016.

[d04p000] The Blitzkrieg Button

question: What year was Playford B Power Station permanently closed in by its Australian operator?
context:
[d07p003] Playford B Power Station
[d07s003] Commissioned in 1963, it was co-located with the larger, newer Northern Power Station.
[d07s004] Playford B was mothballed in 2012 and its permanent closure was announced by operator Alinta Energy in October 2015.
[d07s005] Prior to being mothballed it primarily operated in the summer, when electricity demand peaks.

[d01p000] Playford A Power Station
[d01s000] Playford A power station was the first power station built by the Electricity Trust of South Australia at Port Paterson, South Australia near Port Augusta in South Australia.
[d01s001] It was built in the early 1950s to generate electricity from coal mined from the Telford Cut at Leigh Creek and transported 250 km by rail.
[d01s002] It was joined by the Playford B Power Station soon after, and the Northern Power Station in 1980.

[d04p000] Rugeley power stations
[d04s000] The Rugeley power stations were a series of two coal-fired power stations located on the River Trent at Rugeley in Staffordshire.
[d04s001] The first power station on the site, Rugeley A power station was opened in 1961, but has since been closed and demolished.
[d04s002] Rugeley B power station was commissioned in 1970 and closed on 8 June 2016.

[d06p000] Kosovo A Power Station
[d06s000] Kosovo A Power Station is a lignite power station with five units at Obilić, Kosovo.
[d06s001] It is the second largest power station in Kosovo with capacity of 650 MW after Kosovo B Power Station.
[d06s002] It is described as the worst single-point source of pollution in Europe and it is expected to be closed by 2017.

[d09p003] Dunston Power Station
[d09s003] The first power station built on the site was known as Dunston A Power Station, and the second, which gradually replaced it between 1933 and 1950, was known as Dunston B Power Station.
[d09s004] The A Station was, in its time, one of the largest in the country, and as well as burning coal had early open cycle gas turbine units.
[d09s005] The B Station was the first of a new power station design, and stood as a landmark in the Tyne for over 50 years.

[d05p003] Blyth Power Station
[d05s003] Blyth A Power Station was built and opened first but had a smaller generating capacity than its sister station, Blyth B Power Station, which was built to its west four years later.
[d05s004] The power stations' four large chimneys were a landmark of the Northumberland skyline for over 40 years; the A Station's two chimneys each stood at 140 m ; the B Station's two chimneys were taller, at 170 m each.

[d03p000] Ironbridge power stations
[d03s000] The Ironbridge power stations (also known as the Buildwas power stations) refers to a series of two power stations which have occupied a site on the banks of the River Severn at Buildwas in Shropshire, England.
[d03s001] The Ironbridge B Power Station was operated by E.ON UK but the site is now owned by Uniper.
[d03s002] The station stands near the Ironbridge Gorge World Heritage Site, where the Industrial Revolution began.

[d00p000] Alinta Energy
[d00s000] Alinta Energy is an Australian generation, electricity and gas retailing private company that is owned by Hong Kong-based Chow Tai Fook Enterprises.
[d00s001] Alinta Energy has an owned and contracted generation portfolio of up to 1,957 MW, approximately 800,000 combined electricity and gas retail customers and around 450 employees across Australia and New Zealand.

[d07p000] Playford B Power Station
[d07s000] Playford B Power Station was located at Port Paterson in the Australian state of South Australia about 5.5 km south of the city centre of Port Augusta.
[d07s001] It was coal powered with four 60 MW steam turbines that generate a total of 240 MW of electricity.
[d07s002] Playford B received coal by rail from the Leigh Creek Coal Mine, 280 km to the north and draws cooling water from Spencer Gulf, returning it to the sea at an elevated temperature.

[d09p006] Dunston Power Station
[d09s006] From the A Station's opening in 1910 until the B Station's demolition in 1986, they collectively operated from the early days of electricity generation in the United Kingdom, through the industry's nationalisation, and until a decade before its privatisation.

[d05p000] Shrine Auditorium
[d05s000] The Shrine Auditorium is a landmark large-event venue in Los Angeles, California.
[d05s001] It is also the headquarters of the Al Malaikah Temple, a division of the Shriners.
[d05s002] It was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 139) in 1975.

[d00p000] Birthplace of Adlai E. Stevenson II
[d00s000] Birthplace of Adlai E. Stevenson II is a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 35) in the West Adams neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d00s001] The site was the birthplace of two-time US Presidential candidate Adlai E. Stevenson II, who was born there on February 5, 1900.
[d00s002] The house was designed by C.W. Wedgewood and built in approximately 1894.

[d03p000] Forthmann Carriage House
[d03s000] The Forthmann Carriage House, is a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (No. 103) located in Angelino Heights, Los Angeles, California.
[d03s001] It is a 1,000 sq. ft. Victorian style carriage house built 1882, designed by Burgess J. Reeve.
[d03s002] It was relocated in March 2006 from its original location at 629 West 18th Street.

[d01p003] Elkay Apartments
[d01s003] The building is owned today by his daughter Karen Bruderlin It is next door to the Kelton Apartments designed by Neutra in 1941 for himself.
[d01s004] Despite objections from the owners of the Elkay Apartments, on June 21, 1988, the City of Los Angeles designated the building a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument.

[d09p003] Susana Machado Bernard House and Barn
[d09s003] Noted for its Gothic style with soaring spaces, the house has vaulted ceilings and curved walls.
[d09s004] In 1979, it was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument (HCM #208), and listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
[d09s005] The property was purchased in 1996 by the Center for Human Rights & Constitutional Law.

[d08p000] The Barry Building
[d08s000] The Barry Building is a landmark commercial mid-twentieth century modern building located at 11973 San Vicente Boulevard in the heart of the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d08s001] It was designed by architect Milton Caughey (1911-1958) and completed in 1951.
[d08s002] In 2007, the building was listed as a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument,(Historical Cultural Monument #887), making it one of the few mid-century modern commercial buildings to gain such status.

[d01p000] Elkay Apartments
[d01s000] The Elkay Apartments is an historic five-unit two-story multi-family building located at 638-642 Kelton Avenue, in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles, California.
[d01s001] Designed in 1948 in the international or modernistic style of architecture by noted Los Angeles architect Richard Neutra, it was completed in 1948 for noted violist Louis Kievman.
[d01s002] The name Elkay is derived from his initials.

[d06p009] Powder Magazine (Camp Drum)
[d06s009] When the larger structure was torn down, the Powder Magazine was re-discovered.
[d06s010] In order to save it from demolition, it was declared a Historic-Cultural Monument (HCM #249) in August 1982.
[d06s011] For more than two decades, it has sat on a vacant, fenced-off lot two blocks south of the Drum Barracks.

[d02p000] Millennium Biltmore Hotel
[d02s000] The Millennium Biltmore Hotel, originally named the Los Angeles Biltmore Hotel of the Biltmore Hotels group, is a luxury hotel located across the street from Pershing Square in Downtown Los Angeles, California, US.
[d02s001] Upon its grand opening in 1923, the Los Angeles Biltmore was the largest hotel west of Chicago, Illinois in the United States.
[d02s002] In 1969 the Biltmore Hotel was designated a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument by the City of Los Angeles.

context:
[d01p000] Democratic-Republican Party
[d01s000] The Democratic-Republican Party was an American political party formed by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison in 1791–93 to oppose the centralizing policies of the new Federalist Party run by Alexander Hamilton (1755/57-1804), who was secretary of the treasury and chief architect of George Washington's administration.
[d01s001] The new party controlled the presidency and Congress, as well as most states, from 1801 to 1825, during the First Party System.
[d01s002] It began in 1791 as one faction in Congress, and included many politicians who had been opposed to the new constitution.

[d03p000] Albert Gallatin
[d03s000] Abraham Alfonse Albert Gallatin (January 29, 1761 – August 12, 1849) was a Swiss-American politician, diplomat, ethnologist and linguist.
[d03s001] He was an important leader of the Democratic-Republican Party, serving in various federal elective and appointed positions across four decades.
[d03s002] He represented Pennsylvania in the Senate and the House of Representatives before becoming the longest-tenured United States Secretary of the Treasury and serving as a high-ranking diplomat.

[d01p003] Democratic-Republican Party
[d01s003] They called themselves "Republicans" after their ideology, Republicanism.
[d01s004] They distrusted the Federalist commitment to republicanism.
[d01s005] The party splintered in 1824 into the Jacksonian movement (which became the Democratic Party in 1828) and the short-lived National Republican Party (later succeeded by the Whig Party).

[d02p000] Whig Party (United States)
[d02s000] The Whig Party was a political party active in the middle of the 19th century in the United States.
[d02s001] Four US presidents belonged to the party while in office.
[d02s002] It emerged in the 1830s as the leading opponent of Jacksonians, pulling together former members of the National Republican (one of the successors of the Democratic-Republican Party) and Anti-Masonic Parties.

[d06s001] It marked the beginning of the Second Party System, and the definitive split of the Democratic-Republican Party into the Democratic Party (organized around Andrew Jackson) and the National Republican Party (organized around John Quincy Adams and opponents of Jackson).
[d06s002] While the Democrats cultivated strong local organizations, the National Republicans relied on a clear national platform of high tariffs and internal improvements.

[d00p000] Presidency of Thomas Jefferson
[d00s000] The presidency of Thomas Jefferson began on March 4, 1801, when he was inaugurated as the third President of the United States, and ended on March 4, 1809.
[d00s001] Jefferson assumed the office after defeating incumbent President John Adams in the 1800 presidential election.
[d00s002] The election was a realigning election in which the Democratic-Republican Party swept the Federalist Party out of power, ushering in a generation of Democratic-Republican dominance in American politics.

[d05p003] United States presidential election, 1800
[d05s003] The election was a realigning election that ushered in a generation of Democratic-Republican Party rule and the eventual demise of the Federalist Party in the First Party System.
[d05s004] It was a long, bitter re-match of the 1796 election between the pro-French and pro-decentralization Democratic-Republicans under Jefferson and Aaron Burr and the incumbent Adams and Charles Pinckney's pro-British and pro-centralization Federalists.
[d05s005] The chief political issues revolved around the fallout from the French Revolution, including opposition to the tax imposed by Congress to pay for the mobilization of the new army and the navy in the Quasi-War against France in 1798.

[d02s003] It had distant links to the upscale traditions of the Federalist Party.
[d02s004] Along with the rival Democratic Party, it was central to the Second Party System from the early 1840s to the mid-1860s.
[d02s005] It originally formed in opposition to the policies of President Andrew Jackson (in office 1829–37) and his Democratic Party.

[d00s003] After two terms, Jefferson was succeeded by Secretary of State James Madison, also of the Democratic-Republican Party.

[d08s001] It was ordered by the Ottoman sultan Abdülmecid I (1823-1861), designed by architect Garabet Amira Balyan and completed in 1848.

[d00p000] Clock Tower, Brighton
[d00s000] The Clock Tower (sometimes called the Jubilee Clock Tower) is a free-standing clock tower in the centre of Brighton, part of the English city of Brighton and Hove.
[d00s001] Built in 1888 in commemoration of Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, the distinctive structure included innovative structural features and became a landmark in the popular and fashionable seaside resort.
[d00s002] The city's residents "retain a nostalgic affection" for it, even though opinion is sharply divided as to the tower's architectural merit.

[d04p000] Birgu Clock Tower
[d04s000] The Birgu Clock Tower (Maltese: "It-Torri tal-Arloġġ tal-Birgu" ), also called the "Vittoriosa Clock Tower" and originally the Civic Clock Tower, was a clock tower in Birgu, Malta.
[d04s001] It was located in Victory Square, the city's main square, and it was a prominent landmark in Birgu and the rest of the Three Cities.
[d04s002] The tower was probably built in the Middle Ages, although some sources state that it was constructed in 1549.

[d06p000] Kumanovo Clock Tower
[d06s000] Kumanovo Clock Tower (Macedonian: Саат Кула Куманово ) was a clock tower in Kumanovo, Ottoman Empire (today Republic of Macedonia).
[d06s001] The tower is believed to have existed since the second half of the 18th century but there are now known historical facts.
[d06s002] It was near Eski Mosque in the former Orta Bunar Neighborhood (Macedonian: Орта Бунар Маало ).

[d05p000] Tashkopryu Mosque
[d05s000] Tashkyopryu Mosque (Bulgarian: Ташкьопрю джамия "Tashkyopryu Dzhamiya", Turkish: "Taşköprü Camii") is a mosque in Plovdiv, Bulgaria , built by Ottoman Turks in 16th century during their 500-year rule in today's Bulgaria.
[d05s001] It is currently the third mosque in Plovdiv which is in good condition after Dzhumaya Mosque and Imaret Mosque.
[d05s002] It is currently inactive despite efforts and demands, mainly by Turks of Bulgaria, to give active status for it.

[d09p000] Clock Tower of Murshidabad
[d09s000] The Clock Tower of Murshidabad (locally known just as "Clock Tower" or "Ghari Ghar", also known as "Big Ben of Murshidabad") is a clock tower in the Nizamat Fort Campus in West Bengal, India.
[d09s001] The clock tower stands in the garden space between the Nizamat Imambara and the Hazarduari Palace; to its east, hardly a few feet away, is the old Madina Mosque and the Bacchawali Tope.

[d03p000] Eski Imaret Mosque
[d03s000] Eski Imaret Mosque (Turkish: "Eski Imaret Camii" ) is a former Eastern Orthodox church converted into a mosque by the Ottomans.

[d04p003] Birgu Clock Tower
[d04s003] It served as a watchtower since it had views over the Grand Harbour and the surrounding countryside, and it saw use during the Great Siege of Malta in 1565.

question: Cinnamon sugar is a spice used to flavor this traditional Spanish and Portugese fried pastry.
context:
[d01p000] Cinnamon sugar
[d01s000] Cinnamon sugar is a mixture of ground cinnamon and granulated sugar used as a spice for desserts.
[d01s001] It is commonly used to flavor foods such as Belgian waffles, Snickerdoodle cookies, churros and coffee cake.
[d01s002] It is also found in breakfast cereals such as Cinnamon Toast Crunch.

[d07p000] Churro
[d07s000] A churro (] , ] ) is a fried-dough pastry—predominantly choux—based snack.
[d07s001] Churros are traditional in Spain and Portugal - from where they originate - as well as the Philippines and Ibero-America.
[d07s002] They are also consumed in the Southwestern United States, France and other areas that have received immigration from Spanish and Portuguese-speaking countries.

[d06p000] Cinnamon roll
[d06s000] A cinnamon roll (also cinnamon bun, cinnamon swirl, cinnamon Danish, and cinnamon snail) is a sweet roll served commonly in Northern Europe and North America.
[d06s001] In Denmark, it is the most common form of wienerbrød ('Vienna Bread') and is known as "Kanelsnegl"; 'cinnamon snail'.
[d06s002] In North America, its common use is as breakfast or dessert.

[d02p000] Mixed spice
[d02s000] Mixed spice, also called pudding spice, is a British blend of sweet spices, similar to the pumpkin pie spice used in the United States.
[d02s001] Cinnamon is the dominant flavour, with nutmeg and allspice.
[d02s002] It is often used in baking, or to complement fruits or other sweet foods.

[d05p003] Nuegados
[d05s003] A cinnamon sugar syrup is then poured on top of the dumplings.
[d05s004] They are often eaten with coffee.

[d04p000] Sopaipilla
[d04s000] A sopaipilla, sopapilla, sopaipa, or cachanga is a kind of fried pastry and a type of quick bread served in several regions with Spanish heritage in the Americas.
[d04s001] The word sopaipilla is the diminutive of sopaipa, a word that entered Spanish from the Mozarabic language of Al-Andalus.
[d04s002] The original Mozarabic word "Xopaipa" was used to mean bread soaked in oil, and derived in turn from the Germanic word "suppa" which meant bread soaked in liquid.

[d08p003] Cinnamon leaf oil
[d08s003] It is also used as a source of eugenol for the preparation of synthetic vanillin.
[d08s004] Cinnamon oleoresin obtained by solvent extraction is a dark brown extremely concentrated and viscous liquid, closely approximating the total spice flavour and containing 50% or more volatile oil.
[d08s005] It is used mainly for flavouring food products such as cakes and confectionary.

[d05p000] Nuegados
[d05s000] Nuegados is a traditional plate from many different countries in Latin America.
[d05s001] However, it is only in "El Salvador that they are called 'nuégados'" (Latinaish, Salvadoran Nuegados) Nuegados are "nothing more than fried dumplings coated with a sweet sugar cane sauce".
[d05s002] To prepare nuegados, one deep fries a dough made of corn flour, baking powder, butter, salt, and water in oil.

[d03p000] Cruller
[d03s000] A traditional cruller (or twister) is a fried pastry often made from a rectangle of dough, with a cut made in the middle that allows it to be pulled over and through itself producing twists in the sides of the pastry.
[d03s001] Crullers have been described as resembling "a small, braided torpedo" and having been "a staple of the New England diet since the Pilgrims' day".
[d03s002] Some other cruller styles are made of a denser dough somewhat like that of a cake doughnut formed in a small loaf or stick shape, but not always twisted.

[d08p006] Cinnamon leaf oil
[d08s006] Ground spice has been replaced by oils and oleoresin in food industry.

question: Which 1970's film was released first, Charley and the Angel or The Boatniks?
context:
[d03p000] The Boatniks
[d03s000] The Boatniks is a 1970 American comedy film starring Robert Morse, Stefanie Powers, Don Ameche and Phil Silvers.
[d03s001] It was made by Walt Disney Productions, released by Buena Vista Distribution and directed by Norman Tokar.

[d09p000] Charley and the Angel
[d09s000] Charley and the Angel is a 1973 Disney family/comedy film set in an unidentified small city in the 1930s Depression-era Midwestern United States and starring Fred MacMurray in one of his final film appearances and his last movie for Disney.
[d09s001] The film, directed by Vincent McEveety, is based on "The Golden Evenings of Summer", a 1971 novel written by Will Stanton.

[d06p000] Toys in the Attic (2009 film)
[d06s000] Toys in the Attic (Czech: Na půdě aneb Kdo má dneska narozeniny?
[d06s001] ; festival title: In the Attic: Who Has a Birthday Today?)
[d06s002] is a 2009 Czech-French-Japanese-Slovak primarily stop-motion animated fantasy comedy thriller family film directed by Jiří Barta and written by Edgar Dutka and Barta which depicts a community of toys and other objects in an attic who come to life when no human is around.

[d07p000] Kiss an Angel Good Mornin'
[d07s000] "Kiss an Angel Good Mornin'" is a song written by Ben Peters, and recorded by American country music artist Charley Pride.
[d07s001] It was released in October 1971 as the first single from the album "Charley Pride Sings Heart Songs".
[d07s002] The song has since become one of his signature tunes and was his eighth song to reach number one on the country charts.

question: Are both Dodgy and Massive Attack based in the same country?
context:
[d04p000] Dodgy
[d04s000] Dodgy are an English power pop rock trio, that rose to prominence during the Britpop era of the 1990s.
[d04s001] They are best known for their hits "Staying Out for the Summer", "If You're Thinking of Me", and "Good Enough".
[d04s002] The last was their biggest hit reaching No. 4 in the UK Singles Chart.

[d06p000] The Space Between Us (album)
[d06s000] The Space Between Us is the debut solo album by Craig Armstrong, originally released in 1998 on Melankolic Records.
[d06s001] Elizabeth Fraser of Cocteau Twins contributes vocals to the track "This Love", and The Blue Nile's Paul Buchanan appears on "Let's Go Out Tonight", which is a rework of the song of the same name by Blue Nile.
[d06s002] The first track, "Weather Storm", is a reworking of a song by the same name which appears on Massive Attack's 1994 album, "Protection", to which Armstrong contributed.

[d03p003] Massive Attack
[d03s003] Both "Blue Lines" and "Mezzanine" feature in "Rolling Stone"' s list of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.

[d03p000] Massive Attack
[d03s000] Massive Attack are an English trip hop group formed in 1988 in Bristol, consisting of Robert "3D" Del Naja, Grant "Daddy G" Marshall and formerly Andy "Mushroom" Vowles ("Mush").
[d03s001] Their debut album "Blue Lines" was released in 1991, with the single "Unfinished Sympathy" reaching the charts and later being voted the 63rd greatest song of all time in a poll by "NME".
[d03s002] 1998's "Mezzanine", containing "Teardrop", and 2003's "100th Window" charted in the UK at number one.

[d01p000] Four Walls / Paradise Circus
[d01s000] "Four Walls / Paradise Circus" is a collaboration between Massive Attack and Burial, which was first released as a limited vinyl edition on 17 October 2011, with pre-orders from 10 October 2011.
[d01s001] The single consists of Burial mixes of Massive Attack's previously unreleased track "Four Walls", and of "Paradise Circus", which was featured in their 2010 album "Heligoland".
[d01s002] Both songs featured on the EP contain vocals, and lyrical contributions, by Hope Sandoval of Mazzy Star.

[d09p000] Massive Attack discography
[d09s000] The discography of British trip hop group Massive Attack consists of five studio albums, three compilation albums, five remix albums, one soundtrack album, five extended plays, eighteen singles and twenty-seven music videos.
[d09s001] The group were founded in 1988 by musicians Robert "3D" Del Naja, Grantley "Daddy G" Marshall, Andrew "Mushroom" Vowles and Adrian "Tricky" Thaws in Bristol, England.
[d09s002] Prior to the formation of Massive Attack, all three were members of British sound system The Wild Bunch.

[d02p003] Slo Light
[d02s003] The album was recorded in Christchurch Studios, which is known for the collaboration of Massive Attack and Davidge studios and the recording of the 90's one of the most anticipated album, "Mezzanine".

[d07p000] Massive Attack (song)
[d07s000] "Massive Attack" is a song by Trinidadian rapper Nicki Minaj and American recording artist Sean Garrett.
[d07s001] Written by Minaj, co-written and produced by Garrett and Alex da Kid, "Massive Attack" was released on April 13, 2010.
[d07s002] It was initially intended to be the lead single from Minaj's debut studio album "Pink Friday", but the release was later scrapped in favor of "Your Love".

[d00p000] Protection (Massive Attack song)
[d00s000] "Protection" is a collaboration between Massive Attack and Everything But the Girl singer Tracey Thorn, that appeared on Massive Attack's second album "Protection" on CD and 12" in 1994 as a second single.
[d00s001] It reached number 14 on the UK Singles Chart, staying there for four weeks.
[d00s002] The song was also included on Everything But the Girl's compilations "The Best of" and "Like the Deserts Miss the Rain".

[d07p003] Massive Attack (song)
[d07s003] The song was a distinct change in Minaj's previous work on mixtapes and features, thus receiving mixed to positive reviews from critics, commending lyrical content and distinctiveness, and critiquing that it did not fit her "Barbie" persona well.
[d07s004] An accompanying music video which features a helicopter chase, and militaristic jungle and desert scenes, was positively received.

question: Which breed of dog was first recognized by their country's official kennel club, the American Hairless Terrier or the Saint-Usuge Spaniel?
context:
[d06p000] Saint-Usuge Spaniel
[d06s000] The Saint-Usuge Spaniel (or Épagneul de Saint-Usuge) is a breed of Spaniel originating in the Bresse region of France.
[d06s001] The breed has origins dating back to at least the 16th century, but was nearly extinct by the end of World War II.
[d06s002] Through the efforts of Father Robert Billard, the breed was resurrected during the second half of the 20th century; its national breed club was founded in 1990.

[d06p003] Saint-Usuge Spaniel
[d06s003] The breed was recognised by the Société Centrale Canine (French Kennel Club) in 2003.

[d00p000] American Hairless Terrier
[d00s000] The American Hairless Terrier is a rare breed of dog that was derived as a variant of Rat Terrier.
[d00s001] As of January 1, 2004, the United Kennel Club deemed the AHT a separate terrier breed, granting it full UKC recognition.
[d00s002] An intelligent, social and energetic working breed, the American Hairless Terrier is often listed as a potential good breed choice for allergy sufferers.

[d01p000] American Russell Terrier Club
[d01s000] The American Russell Terrier Club (formerly named the English Jack Russell Terrier Club), founded by JoAnn Stoll in 1995, was the first registry in the United States to maintain the Russell Terrier as a separate breed from the Parson Russell Terrier.
[d01s001] The American Jack Russell Terrier Club is affiliated with both the United Kennel Club and the American Kennel Club.
[d01s002] The purpose of the early founders was to establish a registry for the perpetuation and development of the Russell Terrier as a pure strain of working Jack Russell Terrier keeping their blood and type pure within the registry to works towards Kennel Club recognition as an official breed in the US.

Welsh Springer Spaniel
The Welsh Springer Spaniel is a breed of dog and a member of the spaniel family. Thought to be comparable to the old Land Spaniel, they are similar to the English Springer Spaniel and historically have been referred to as both the Welsh Spaniel and the Welsh Cocker Spaniel. They were relatively unknown until a succession of victories in dog trials by the breed increased its popularity.

question: What year was Playford B Power Station permanently closed in by its Australian operator?
context:

[d07p000] Playford B Power Station
[d07s000] Playford B Power Station was located at Port Paterson in the Australian state of South Australia about 5.5 km south of the city centre of Port Augusta.
[d07s001] It was coal powered with four 60 MW steam turbines that generate a total of 240 MW of electricity.
[d07s002] Playford B received coal by rail from the Leigh Creek Coal Mine, 280 km to the north and draws cooling water from Spencer Gulf, returning it to the sea at an elevated temperature.

[d01p000] Playford A Power Station
[d01s000] Playford A power station was the first power station built by the Electricity Trust of South Australia at Port Paterson, South Australia near Port Augusta in South Australia.
[d01s001] It was built in the early 1950s to generate electricity from coal mined from the Telford Cut at Leigh Creek and transported 250 km by rail.
[d01s002] It was joined by the Playford B Power Station soon after, and the Northern Power Station in 1980.

[d06p000] Kosovo A Power Station
[d06s000] Kosovo A Power Station is a lignite power station with five units at Obilić, Kosovo.
[d06s001] It is the second largest power station in Kosovo with capacity of 650 MW after Kosovo B Power Station.
[d06s002] It is described as the worst single-point source of pollution in Europe and it is expected to be closed by 2017.

question: In what order does Three Colours: Blue appear in the Three Colours trilogy?
context:
[d04p000] Three Colours: Blue
[d04s000] Three Colours: Blue (French: Trois couleurs : Bleu ) is a 1993 French drama film directed and co-written by Polish filmmaker Krzysztof Kieślowski.
[d04s001] "Blue" is the first of three films that comprise the "Three Colours" trilogy, themed on the French Revolutionary ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity; it is followed by "" and "".
[d04s002] According to Kieślowski, the subject of the film is liberty, specifically emotional liberty, rather than its social or political meaning.

[d06p000] Three Colours trilogy
[d06s000] The "Three Colours" trilogy (Polish: "Trzy kolory" , French: "Trois couleurs" ) is a three-part film series directed by Krzysztof Kieślowski.
[d06s001] Two of the films were made in French and one primarily in Polish: "" (1993), "" (1994), and "" (1994).
[d06s002] All three were co-written by Kieślowski and Krzysztof Piesiewicz (with story consultants Agnieszka Holland and Sławomir Idziak) and have musical scores by Zbigniew Preisner.

[d00p000] Three Colours: White
[d00s000] Three Colours: White (French: Trois couleurs : Blanc ) is a 1994 French-Polish comedy-drama film co-written, produced, and directed by Krzysztof Kieślowski.
[d00s001] "White" is the second in "The Three Colors Trilogy", themed on the French Revolutionary ideals, following "" and preceding "".
[d00s002] The film was selected as the Polish entry for the Best Foreign Language Film at the 67th Academy Awards, but was not accepted as a nominee.

[d05p003] Blue
[d05s003] In painting and traditional colour theory, blue is one of the three primary colours of pigments, along with red and yellow, which can be mixed to form a wide gamut of colours.
[d05s004] Red and blue mixed together form violet, blue and yellow together form green.
[d05s005] Blue is also a primary colour in the RGB colour model, used to create all the colours on the screen of a television or computer monitor.

[d08p000] Pan-African colours
[d08s000] The term Pan-African colours refers to two different sets of three colours: red, gold (not yellow), and green (inspired by the flag of Ethiopia), and red, black, and green.
[d08s001] They are used in flags and other emblems of various countries and territories in Africa and the Americas to represent Pan-Africanist ideology.
[d08s002] The Rastafarian movement and many Pan-African organisations also often employ the colours for their activities.

[d09p000] Requiem for my friend (Preisner)
[d09s000] Requiem for my friend is a major and the first non-film musical work composed by Zbigniew Preisner.
[d09s001] The composition was meant to honour the composer's late friend, the director Krzysztof Kieślowski, with whom he collaborated while working on a number of films, including the famous "Three Colours" trilogy.
[d09s002] The album was released in 1998 although some parts of the work must have been ready upon Kieślowski's passing as Preisner asserted in an interview that "the Requiem had accompanied Krzysztof in his last journey".

[d01p003] Be All That You Can't Be
[d01s003] The vinyl is available in three colours: Blue, orange and white (Hot Topic Exclusive).
[d01s004] Each colour is limited to 500.
[d01s005] The music video for the song was released through Absolute Punk on 6 August 2009.

[d07p000] City of Sydney flag
[d07s000] The City of Sydney flag is made up of a horizontal triband of three colours – white, gold and blue.
[d07s001] It was designed in 1908.
[d07s002] The top third of the flag features three designs.

[d03p003] Hokusai Manga
[d03s003] Block-printed in three colours (black, gray and pale flesh), the Manga comprise literally thousands of images in 15 volumes, the first published in 1814, when the artist was 55.
[d03s004] The final three volumes were published posthumously, two of them assembled by their publisher from previously unpublished material.
[d03s005] The final volume was made up of previously published works, some not even by Hokusai, and is not considered authentic by art historians.

[d05p000] Blue
[d05s000] Blue is the colour between violet and green on the spectrum of visible light.
[d05s001] Human eyes perceive blue when observing light with a wavelength between 450 and 495 nanometres. Blues with a higher frequency and thus a shorter wavelength appear more violet, while those with a lower frequency and a longer wavelength gradually appear more green.
[d05s002] Pure blue, in the middle, has a wavelength of 470 nanometres.

question: Are Power Grid and Vanished Planet both cooperative board games?
context:
[d00p000] Vanished Planet
[d00s000] Vanished Planet is a cooperative board game that debuted at the World Boardgaming Championships in 2003.
[d00s001] "Vanished Planet" pits the players against a time limit; the players must succeed in a certain number of goals before this time limit is reached, or they all lose.

[d08p000] Power Grid
[d08s000] Power Grid is the English-language edition of the multiplayer German-style board game Funkenschlag (in its second incarnation) designed by Friedemann Friese and first published in 2004.
[d08s001] Power Grid is published by Rio Grande Games.

[d07p000] Power Grid Corporation of India
[d07s000] The Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID), (, ) is an Indian state-owned electric utilities company headquartered in Gurugram, India.
[d07s001] POWERGRID transmits about 50% of the total power generated in India on its transmission network.
[d07s002] Its former subsidiary company, Power System Operation Corporation Limited (POSOCO) handles power management for Power Grid.

[d05p000] Pandemic (board game)
[d05s000] Pandemic is a cooperative board game designed by Matt Leacock and published by Z-Man Games in 2007.
[d05s001] "Pandemic" is based on the premise that four diseases have broken out in the world, each threatening to wipe out a region.
[d05s002] The game accommodates 2 to 4 players, each playing one of five possible specialists: dispatcher, medic, scientist, researcher, or operations expert.

[d05p003] Pandemic (board game)
[d05s003] The game is unlike most board games in that the gameplay is cooperative, rather than competitive.
[d05s004] Through the combined effort of all the players, the goal is to discover all four cures before any of several game-losing conditions are reached.

[d02p000] National Grid Corporation of the Philippines
[d02s000] The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is a private company that was created on January 15, 2009 through RA 9511.
[d02s001] It is a consortium of 3 corporations, namely Monte Oro Grid Resources Corporation, Calaca High Power Corporation, and the State Grid Corporation of China.
[d02s002] As the franchise holder, it is in charge of operating, managing, maintaining, and expanding the country's Philippine government or state-owned (through National Transmission Corporation or TransCo) power grid, controls the supply and demand of power by determining the power mix through the selection of power plants to put online (i.e., to signal power plants to produce power, as power plants will only produce power or feed their power to the transmission grid when directed by NGCP).

[d09p000] Dynamic demand (electric power)
[d09s000] Dynamic Demand is the name of a semi-passive technology for adjusting load demands on an electrical power grid.
[d09s001] (It is also the name of an independent not-for-profit organization in the UK supported by a charitable grant from the Esmée Fairbairn Foundation dedicated to promoting this technology.)
[d09s002] The concept is that by monitoring the frequency of the power grid, as well as their own controls, intermittent domestic and industrial loads switch themselves on/off at optimal moments to balance the overall grid load with generation, reducing critical power mismatches.

[d07p003] Power Grid Corporation of India
[d07s003] POWERGRID also operates a telecom business under the name POWERTEL.
[d07s004] Shri I S Jha, an alumnus of National Institute of Technology, Jamshedpur serves as the Chairman and Managing Director of the company.

[d03p000] Power Grid Company of Bangladesh
[d03s000] Power Grid Company of Bangladesh is the sole electric power transmission organization in Bangladesh.
[d03s001] It is a government company that owns and operates the power grid in Bangladesh.
[d03s002] It is a subsidiary of Power Development Board.

[d04p003] Advanced Distribution Automation
[d04s003] Electric power transmission systems typically operate above 110kV, whereas Electricity distribution systems operate at lower voltages.
[d04s004] Normally, electric utilities with SCADA systems have extensive control over transmission-level equipment, and increasing control over distribution-level equipment via distribution automation.
[d04s005] However, they often are unable to control smaller entities such as Distributed energy resources (DERs), buildings, and homes.

question: In what city can a person find both the Nusretiye Clock Tower and the Eski Imaret Mosque be found?
context:
[d08p000] Nusretiye Clock Tower
[d08s000] Nusretiye Clock Tower, aka Tophane Clock Tower, is a clock tower situated in Tophane, a neighborhood in Beyoğlu district of Istanbul, Turkey next to Nusretiye Mosque and Tophane Kiosk at the European waterfront of Bosphorus.
[d08s001] It was ordered by the Ottoman sultan Abdülmecid I (1823-1861), designed by architect Garabet Amira Balyan and completed in 1848.

[d03p000] Eski Imaret Mosque
[d03s000] Eski Imaret Mosque (Turkish: "Eski Imaret Camii" ) is a former Eastern Orthodox church converted into a mosque by the Ottomans.
[d03s001] The church has traditionally been identified with that belonging to the Monastery of Christ Pantepoptes (Greek: Μονή του Χριστού Παντεπόπτη ), meaning "Christ the all-seeing".
[d03s002] It is the only documented 11th-century church in Istanbul which survives intact, and represents a key monument of middle Byzantine architecture.

[d06p000] Kumanovo Clock Tower
[d06s000] Kumanovo Clock Tower (Macedonian: Саат Кула Куманово ) was a clock tower in Kumanovo, Ottoman Empire (today Republic of Macedonia).
[d06s001] The tower is believed to have existed since the second half of the 18th century but there are now known historical facts.
[d06s002] It was near Eski Mosque in the former Orta Bunar Neighborhood (Macedonian: Орта Бунар Маало ).

[d09p000] Clock Tower of Murshidabad
[d09s000] The Clock Tower of Murshidabad (locally known just as "Clock Tower" or "Ghari Ghar", also known as "Big Ben of Murshidabad") is a clock tower in the Nizamat Fort Campus in West Bengal, India.
[d09s001] The clock tower stands in the garden space between the Nizamat Imambara and the Hazarduari Palace; to its east, hardly a few feet away, is the old Madina Mosque and the Bacchawali Tope.

[d07p000] Hysen Pasha Mosque
[d07s000] Hysen Pasha Mosque (Albanian: "Xhamia e Hysen Pashës" ) or Clock Mosque "(Xhamia e Sahatit)" is a Cultural Monument of Albania, located in Berat.
[d07s001] It was built in 1670 by Hussein Pasha.
[d07s002] It is named Clock Mosque because in 1870 the Ottomans built a clock tower next to it.

[d00p000] Clock Tower, Brighton
[d00s000] The Clock Tower (sometimes called the Jubilee Clock Tower) is a free-standing clock tower in the centre of Brighton, part of the English city of Brighton and Hove.
[d00s001] Built in 1888 in commemoration of Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, the distinctive structure included innovative structural features and became a landmark in the popular and fashionable seaside resort.
[d00s002] The city's residents "retain a nostalgic affection" for it, even though opinion is sharply divided as to the tower's architectural merit.

[d07s003] The clock tower was destroyed during the Communist dictatorship in 1967.
[d07s004] The mosque also got destroyed with the minaret being the only part left over.
[d07s005] After the end of Communism the mosque got renovated.

[d04s001] It was located in Victory Square, the city's main square, and it was a prominent landmark in Birgu and the rest of the Three Cities.
[d04s002] The tower was probably built in the Middle Ages, although some sources state that it was constructed in 1549.
