question: What company was Luca Cordero di Montezemolo the chairman of that merged into a new Netherlands-based holding company Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV?
context:
[d05p000] Fiat S.p.A.
[d05s000] Fiat S.p.A., or "Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino" (Italian Automobile Factory of Turin), was an Italian holding company whose original and core activities were in the automotive industry, and that was succeeded by Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (FCA).
[d05s001] The Fiat Group contained many brands such as Ferrari, Maserati, Fiat, Alfa Romeo, the Chrysler Group, and many more.
[d05s002] On 29 January 2014, it was announced that Fiat S.p.A. (the former owner of Fiat Group) was to be merged into a new Netherlands-based holding company Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (FCA), took place before the end of 2014.

[d01p000] Fiat Chrysler Automobiles
[d01s000] Fiat Chrysler Automobiles N.V. (abbreviated as FCA) is an Italian-controlled multinational corporation incorporated in the Netherlands, and currently the world’s seventh-largest auto maker.
[d01s001] The group was established in late 2014 by merging Fiat S.p.A. into a new holding company, FCA (with headquarters in London) for tax purposes.
[d01s002] The holding company is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and Borsa Italiana in Milan.

[d02p000] Fiat Industrial
[d02s000] Fiat Industrial S.p.A. was an Italian company into which Fiat S.p.A. (parent company of Fiat Group) demerged most of its activities not directly related to automobiles at the start of 2011.
[d02s001] Fiat Industrial served as a holding company for the activities of truck manufacturer Iveco; an 89.3% stake in the agricultural and construction equipment producer CNH Global; and FPT Industrial, which consists of the industrial and marine activities formerly part of Fiat Powertrain Technologies.
[d02s002] The company's Chairman was Sergio Marchionne, who also served as CEO of Fiat S.p.A. and Chairman/CEO of Chrysler Group LLC, now merged as Fiat Chrysler Automobiles.

[d07p000] Luca Cordero di Montezemolo
[d07s000] Luca Cordero di Montezemolo (] ; born 31 August 1947) is an Italian businessman, former Chairman of Ferrari, and formerly Chairman of Fiat S.p.A. and President of Confindustria and FIEG.
[d07s001] He comes from an aristocratic family from the region of Piedmont in Italy.
[d07s002] He graduated with a degree in law from La Sapienza University in 1971.

[d06p000] Future Italy
[d06s000] Future Italy ("Italia Futura", IF) is an Italian liberal-centrist think tank, formed in 2009 by Luca Cordero di Montezemolo, chairman of Alitalia (since 2014) and former chairman of Ferrari (1991–2014), FIAT (2004–2010) and Confindustria (2004–2008).

[d08p000] Ferrari Ascari
[d08s000] The Ferrari Ascari is a Ferrari concept car that won the "Ferrari: New Concepts for the Myth" car design competition in 2005.
[d08s001] The car was designed by Manuele Amprimo, Werner Gruber, and Yu Jae-Cheul from Istituto Europeo di Design (IED; English: "European Institute of Design"), Turin, Italy.
[d08s002] The judges of the competition included Luca Cordero di Montezemolo, the second and only living son of Enzo Ferrari, Piero Ferrari, Jean Todt, Amedeo Felisa, Massimo Fumarola, Pininfarina, and more than 22,000 users of FerrariWorld's online website.

[d03p000] 2009 24 Hours of Le Mans
[d03s000] The 2009 24 Hours of Le Mans (French: "24 Heures du Mans 2009" ) was the 77th Grand Prix of Endurance, an endurance auto race run over 24 hours.
[d03s001] It took place at the Circuit de la Sarthe, Le Mans, France, and was organised by the Automobile Club de l'Ouest (ACO) over 13–14 June 2009 and was started by Fiat and Ferrari chairman Luca Cordero di Montezemolo at 15:00 local time (13:00 UTC).
[d03s002] A test day was initially scheduled for 31 May that year, but was canceled by the ACO due to economic concerns.

[d04p000] GAC Fiat
[d04s000] GAC Fiat Chrysler Automobiles Co., Ltd. is an automobile manufacturing company headquartered in Changsha, China and a 50:50 joint-venture between GAC Group and Fiat Chrysler Automobiles.
[d04s001] The company was founded on 9 March 2010.
[d04s002] Fiat has agreed to invest an initial US$559 million in the venture.

[d05p003] Fiat S.p.A.
[d05s003] Fiat Chrysler Automobiles became the new owner of Fiat Group.
[d05s004] On 1 August 2014, Fiat S.p.A. received necessary shareholder approval to proceed with the merger (which followed board approval).
[d05s005] The merger became effective 12 October 2014.

[d07p003] Luca Cordero di Montezemolo
[d07s003] Afterward, he studied for a masters degree in international commercial law at Columbia University.
[d07s004] He is one of the founders and former president of NTV, an Italian company which is Europe's first private open access operator of 300 km/h (186 mph) high-speed trains.

[d09s000] Divine Trash is a 1998 documentary film directed by Steve Yeager about the life and work of John Waters.

[d01p000] Zoo (2007 film)
[d01s000] Zoo is a 2007 American documentary film based on the life and death of Kenneth Pinyan, an American man who died of peritonitis due to perforation of the colon after engaging in an unusual tryst involving receptive anal sex with a horse.
[d01s001] The film's public debut was at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2007, where it was one of 16 winners out of 856 candidates.
[d01s002] Following Sundance, it was selected as one of the top five American films to be presented at the Directors' Fortnight sidebar at the 2007 Cannes Film Festival.

[d00s004] It led to his first documentary ‘Pala’.
[d00s005] He continued to make short experimental works and documenting arts/artists for the next few years.

[d03p000] Documentary mode
[d03s000] Documentary mode is a conceptual scheme developed by American documentary theorist Bill Nichols that seeks to distinguish particular traits and conventions of various documentary film styles.
[d03s001] Nichols identifies six different documentary 'modes' in his schema: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive, and performative.
[d03s002] While Nichols' discussion of modes does progress chronologically with the order of their appearance in practice, documentary film often returns to themes and devices from previous modes.

[d05p000] Clifford Vaughs
[d05s000] Clifford A. 'Soney' Vaughs (April 16, 1937 – July 2, 2016) was an American civil rights activist, filmmaker, and motorcycle builder.
[d05s001] Vaughs designed the two chopper motorcycles used for the 1969 film 'Easy Rider', while an Associate Producer on the film.
[d05s002] He also produced and directed the documentary 'What Will the Harvest Be?'

[d03p006] Documentary mode
[d03s006] As Nichols points out, "the characteristics of a given mode function as a dominant in a given film…but they do not dictate or determine every aspect of its organization."
[d03s007] (Nichols 2001)

[d00s008] His latest film is 'infiltrator' starring Veer Rajwant Singh which is a 15 minute short story in an international omnibus called 'In the same garden'

[d03s003] Therefore, it is inaccurate to think of modes as historical punctuation marks in an evolution towards an ultimate accepted documentary style.
[d03s004] Also, modes are not mutually exclusive.
[d03s005] There is often significant overlapping between modalities within individual documentary features.

[d07s002] He is the writer of Doctor Who stories 'The Memory Bank' and 'The Middle' for Big Finish.

[d08s000] Small Teen, Bigger World was a four-part documentary following the life of a teenager with dwarfism, Jasmine Burkitt, and details her family and life.
[d08s001] It was the second series to follow Jasmine's life, following the hour-long documentary 'Small Teen, Big World', which aired in July 2010.

question: Were both the Battle of Stones River and the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River fought in the 19th century?
context:
[d06p000] Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River
[d06s000] The Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River, also known as the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on () or the Second Phase Campaign Western Sector (), was a decisive battle in the Korean War, and it took place from November 25 to December 2, 1950, along the Ch'ongch'on River Valley in the northwestern part of North Korea.
[d06s001] In response to the successful Chinese First Phase Campaign against the United Nations forces, General Douglas MacArthur launched the Home-by-Christmas Offensive to evict the Chinese forces from Korea and to end the war.
[d06s002] Anticipating this reaction, the Chinese People's Volunteer Army Commander Peng Dehuai planned a counteroffensive, dubbed the "Second Phase Campaign", against the advancing UN forces.

[d04p000] Battle of Stones River
[d04s000] The Battle of Stones River or Second Battle of Murfreesboro, was fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863, in Middle Tennessee, as the culmination of the Stones River Campaign in the Western Theater of the American Civil War.
[d04s001] Of the major battles of the Civil War, Stones River had the highest percentage of casualties on both sides.
[d04s002] Although the battle itself was inconclusive, the Union Army's repulse of two Confederate attacks and the subsequent Confederate withdrawal were a much-needed boost to Union morale after the defeat at the Battle of Fredericksburg, and it dashed Confederate aspirations for control of Middle Tennessee.

[d03p003] Umba River (Tanzania)
[d03s003] Just before the Umba flows into the Indian Ocean, it crosses the border to Kenya.
[d03s004] The mouth itself marks the most eastern point on the border between Tanzania and Kenya, which was largely made in a straight line to the northwest towards Lake Victoria in the 19th Century.
[d03s005] On the upper reaches of the river in the mid-1960s rich deposits of precious stones, including sapphires and Spessartine, were discovered.

[d03p003] Ernst Abbe
[d03s003] He was a co-owner of Carl Zeiss AG, a German manufacturer of research microscopes, astronomical telescopes, planetariums and other optical systems.

[d07p000] Abbe error
[d07s000] Abbe error, named after Ernst Abbe, also called sine error, describes the magnification of angular error over distance.
[d07s001] For example, when one measures a point that is 1 meter away at 45 degrees, an angular error of 1 degree corresponds to a positional error of over 1.745 cm, equivalent to a distance-measurement error of 1.745%.

[d00p000] Porro–Abbe prism
[d00s000] A Porro–Abbe prism (sometimes called a Abbe–Porro prism), named for Ignazio Porro and Ernst Abbe, is a type of reflection prism used in some optical instruments to alter the orientation of an image.
[d00s001] It is a variant of the more common double Porro prism configuration.

[d09p003] Othello error
[d09s003] The error is named after William Shakespeare's tragic play "Othello"; the dynamics between the two main characters, Othello and Desdemona are a particularly notable example of the error in practice.

[d06p000] Ernst-Abbe-Sportfeld
[d06s000] Ernst Abbe Sportfield is a sports facility in Jena, Germany.
[d06s001] It was dedicated on August 24, 1924 and was named after entrepreneur Ernst Abbe 15 years later.
[d06s002] The facility is in southern Jena, directly on the Saale River.

[d02p000] Description error
[d02s000] A description error or selection error is an error, or more specifically a human error, that occurs when a person performs the correct action on the wrong object due to insufficient specification of an action which would have led to a desired result.
[d02s001] This commonly happens when similar actions lead to different results.
[d02s002] A typical example is a panel with rows of identical switches, where it is easy to carry out a correct action (flip a switch) on a wrong switch due to their insufficient differentiation.

[d08p000] Bramble–Hilbert lemma
[d08s000] In mathematics, particularly numerical analysis, the Bramble–Hilbert lemma, named after James H. Bramble and Stephen Hilbert, bounds the error of an approximation of a function formula_1 by a polynomial of order at most formula_2 in terms of derivatives of formula_1 of order formula_4.
[d08s001] Both the error of the approximation and the derivatives of formula_1 are measured by formula_6 norms on a bounded domain in formula_7.
[d08s002] This is similar to classical numerical analysis, where, for example, the error of linear interpolation formula_1 can be bounded using the second derivative of formula_1.

[d05p000] Errors of impunity
[d05s000] Errors of impunity is a term used in Brian Forst's book "Errors of Justice" and in Robert Bohm's introduction to a special edition of "The Journal of Criminal Justice" on miscarriages of justice.
[d05s001] They are defined as lapses that result in criminals either remaining at large or receiving sanctions that are below a socially optimal level.
[d05s002] If convicting an innocent person, called a miscarriage of justice, is a Type I error for falsely identifying culpability (a "false positive"), then an error of impunity would be a Type II error of failing to find a culpable person guilty (a "false negative").

[d04p000] Van Abbemuseum
[d04s000] Van Abbemuseum (] ) is a museum of modern and contemporary art located in central Eindhoven, Netherlands, on the east bank of the Dommel river.
[d04s001] Established in 1936, the Abbe Museum is named after its founder, Henri van Abbe.
[d04s002] Van Abbe was a lover of modern art and wanted to enjoy it there from Eindhoven.

[d03p000] Ernst Abbe
[d03s000] Ernst Karl Abbe HonFRMS (23 January 1840 – 14 January 1905) was a German physicist, optical scientist, entrepreneur, and social reformer.
[d03s001] Together with Otto Schott and Carl Zeiss, he laid the foundation of modern optics.
[d03s002] Abbe developed numerous optical instruments.

This commonly happens when similar actions lead to different results. A typical example is a panel with rows of identical switches, where it is easy to carry out a correct action (flip a switch) on a wrong switch due to their insufficient differentiation.

facts.title: Errors of impunity

question: Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria that stretches from Stonethwaite which is a part of a valley and civil parrish in what Borough?
context:
[d06p000] Glaramara
[d06s000] Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria.
[d06s001] It is a substantial fell that is part of a long ridge that stretches for over six kilometres from Stonethwaite in Borrowdale up to the important mountain pass of Esk Hause.
[d06s002] The summit of Glaramara at 783 m (2,569 ft) is the central point of this ridge, which separates the valleys of Langstrath and Grains Gill.

[d01p000] Borrowdale
[d01s000] Borrowdale is a valley and civil parish in the English Lake District in the Borough of Allerdale in Cumbria, England.

[d04p000] Stonethwaite
[d04s000] Stonethwaite is a small village in the Lake District in the English county of Cumbria.
[d04s001] Historically part of Cumberland, it is situated in the valley of the Stonethwaite Beck, a side valley of Borrowdale, and within the Lake District National Park.
[d04s002] It is on the Cumbria Way long distance footpath.

[d09p000] Eagle Crag
[d09s000] Eagle Crag is a fell in the Lake District in Cumbria, England, it is situated near the village of Stonethwaite where the valleys of Langstrath and Greenup join.
[d09s001] Impressive walls of crag look down upon Stonethwaite, making Eagle Crag the most arresting sight from that settlement.
[d09s002] It can be climbed direct by the average walker, picking a route between the rock faces.

[d00p003] Ritson's Force
[d00s003] Ritsons Force and Wasdale Head are in the Lake District National Park which is in Cumbria, an English county that borders with Scotland

[d03p000] Great Crag
[d03s000] Great Crag is a fell in the English Lake District, located near the hamlets of Rosthwaite and Stonethwaite in Borrowdale.

[d00p000] Ritson's Force
[d00s000] Ritson's Force is a set of waterfalls in the valley of Mosedale in the English Lake District.
[d00s001] It is also the river that leads past the Wasdale Head Inn and the Great Gable Brewing Company.
[d00s002] The hills nearby include Sca Fell and Scafell Pike, England's two highest mountains, and Great Gable, home to British climbing.

[d02p000] Blindcrake
[d02s000] Blindcrake is a village and civil parish within the Isel Valley, in the Lake District National Park and in the Allerdale district of Cumbria, England.
[d02s001] According to the 2001 census it had a population of 287, increasing to 348 at the 2011 Census.
[d02s002] The parish includes Blindcrake village and the hamlets of Redmain, Isel and Sunderland, The whole parish lies within the Lake District National Park and, since 2001, Blindcrake village  is one of 23 designated conservation areas of the National Park Planning Authority.

[d05p000] Dock Tarn
[d05s000] Dock Tarn is a small tarn located within the Lake District National Park in Cumbria, England at grid reference [ NY273143] .
[d05s001] It is situated on moorland at 400 metres above sea level near the summit of Great Crag, midway between Watendlath, the Stonethwaite valley and Borrowdale.
[d05s002] It measures approximately 300 by 200 metres, and the shoreline is indented with rocky headlands and bays.

[d02p003] Blindcrake
[d02s003] This status is largely based on its mediaeval strip field pattern which is described as "undoubtedly the finest example of its type in the Lake District".
[d02s004] The parish boundary is approximately defined by the Lake District National Park boundary in the north and west, by a line 2 km to the west of the A591 in the east and by the River Derwent in the south.
[d02s005] It is one of the smallest parishes within the Allerdale district of Cumbria.

context:
[d01p000] Fiat Chrysler Automobiles
[d01s000] Fiat Chrysler Automobiles N.V. (abbreviated as FCA) is an Italian-controlled multinational corporation incorporated in the Netherlands, and currently the world’s seventh-largest auto maker.
[d01s001] The group was established in late 2014 by merging Fiat S.p.A. into a new holding company, FCA (with headquarters in London) for tax purposes.
[d01s002] The holding company is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and Borsa Italiana in Milan.

[d05p000] Fiat S.p.A.
[d05s000] Fiat S.p.A., or "Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino" (Italian Automobile Factory of Turin), was an Italian holding company whose original and core activities were in the automotive industry, and that was succeeded by Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (FCA).
[d05s001] The Fiat Group contained many brands such as Ferrari, Maserati, Fiat, Alfa Romeo, the Chrysler Group, and many more.
[d05s002] On 29 January 2014, it was announced that Fiat S.p.A. (the former owner of Fiat Group) was to be merged into a new Netherlands-based holding company Fiat Chrysler Automobiles NV (FCA), took place before the end of 2014.

[d02p000] Fiat Industrial
[d02s000] Fiat Industrial S.p.A. was an Italian company into which Fiat S.p.A. (parent company of Fiat Group) demerged most of its activities not directly related to automobiles at the start of 2011.
[d02s001] Fiat Industrial served as a holding company for the activities of truck manufacturer Iveco; an 89.3% stake in the agricultural and construction equipment producer CNH Global; and FPT Industrial, which consists of the industrial and marine activities formerly part of Fiat Powertrain Technologies.
[d02s002] The company's Chairman was Sergio Marchionne, who also served as CEO of Fiat S.p.A. and Chairman/CEO of Chrysler Group LLC, now merged as Fiat Chrysler Automobiles.

question: What genre of music was played by both Tappi Tíkarrass and INXS?
context:
[d02p000] Tappi Tíkarrass
[d02s000] Tappi Tíkarrass was an Icelandic punk band which added elements of funk, rock and jazz to their music, marking a difference from other traditional bands at that time.
[d02s001] The band is also considered the first serious music project of now renowned singer Björk Guðmundsdóttir.

[d09p000] Miranda (album)
[d09s000] Miranda is the only studio album by Icelandic punk band Tappi Tíkarrass.
[d09s001] It was released on December 23, 1983 through Gramm.

[d04p000] Nýtt líf
[d04s000] Nýtt Líf (   , English: "New Life") is an Icelandic film directed by Þráinn Bertelsson and released in 1983.
[d04s001] The film is a comedy shot in the Westman Islands and stars Eggert Þorleifsson and Karl Ágúst Úlfsson, among others.
[d04s002] The music features several musicians including the band Tappi Tíkarrass (of which Björk was a member), which contributed the songs "Sperglar" and "Kukl" (a.k.a. "Seiður").

[d00p000] Bitið fast í vitið
[d00s000] Bitið fast í vitið (roughly "Bite Hard In Your Mind" in Icelandic) is the début EP of Icelander punk/pop group Tappi Tíkarrass .
[d00s001] It was released in late-1982 on the Spor label, within a year of the band's formation in September 1981 – led by vocalists Björk and Eyþór Arnalds .
[d00s002] This was the band's most punk-oriented release and contains five tracks, featuring one in English, "London".

[d03p003] INXS
[d03s003] For twenty years, INXS was fronted by Hutchence, whose "sultry good looks" and magnetic stage presence made him the focal point of the band.
[d03s004] Initially known for their new wave/pop style, the band later developed a harder pub rock style that included funk and dance elements.

[d07p000] Rave music
[d07s000] Rave music may either refer to the late 1980s/early 1990s genres of house, breakbeat, acid house, techno and hardcore techno, which were the first genres of music to be played at rave parties, or to any other genre of electronic dance music (EDM) that may be played at a rave.
[d07s001] The genre "rave", also known as hardcore by early ravers, first appeared amongst the UK "acid" movement during the late 1980s at warehouse parties and other underground venues, as well as on UK pirate radio stations.
[d07s002] The genre would develop into oldschool hardcore, which lead onto newer forms of rave music such as drum and bass and 2-step, as well as other hardcore techno genres, such as gabber, hardstyle and happy hardcore.

[d05p003] Disco polo
[d05s003] Disco polo have enjoyed a renaissance of popularity in late 2007.
[d05s004] Language Dictionary Polish Publishing PWN defines the genre as a Polish variant of disco music, with simple melodies.
[d05s005] It is derived from disco, Euro disco contemporary folk music influenced by Italo disco and Polish folk songs (specifically, the vulgarized subgenre of which is mostly played at weddings and feasts).

[d01p003] Steeltown (band)
[d01s003] The group members were Andy Richmond vocals, Peter Howard keyboards, Terry Gidman drums and Kate Richmond vocals and percussion and Reece Speceis Lead Guitar.
[d01s004] The band were formed from the remnant members of a Scottish group called the Technicians who migrated to Australia in the 80s and who also attained top 40 status with their music releases, Hot for Love, Clockwork Clown and Sodier of Fortune through record companies Powderworks, EMI and BMG, and were published by MMA which was owned by legendary rock outfit INXS.

[d08p000] Folk rock
[d08s000] Folk rock is a music genre combining elements of folk music and rock music.
[d08s001] In its earliest and narrowest sense, the term referred to a genre that arose in the United States and the United Kingdom around the mid-1960s.
[d08s002] The genre emerged from bands such as the Beatles, the Searchers, and the Animals in the UK, and Bob Dylan and the Byrds in the US, who played traditional folk music and songs with rock instrumentation.

[d06p003] Kidandali
[d06s003] The music itself is given this name because most times it is the kind of music played or performed at such local parties and functions.
[d06s004] Some other sources and commentators refer to the genre alternatively as "Band music" while others refer to it as "Afrobeat".

question: Who is the host of Wall of Fame known for his partnership with?
context:
[d07p000] Wall of Fame (game show)
[d07s000] Wall of Fame is a British comedy panel game that was first broadcast on Sky1 in 2011.
[d07s001] It is hosted by "Little Britain" star David Walliams and features Jack Dee, Kate Garraway, with Tamara Ecclestone for the first two episodes then Sara Pascoe took over from episode three, and Andrew Maxwell as regular panellists, alongside two weekly guests.

[d06p000] David Walliams
[d06s000] David Edward Williams, OBE (born 20 August 1971), known professionally as David Walliams ( ), is an English comedian, actor, talent-show judge, author, presenter, and activist, known for his partnership with Matt Lucas on the BBC One sketch show "Little Britain."

[d01p000] Montel Williams
[d01s000] Montel Brian Anthony Williams (born July 3, 1956) is an American television personality, radio talk show host, and actor.
[d01s001] He is best known as host of the long-running "The Montel Williams Show", and more recently as a spokesman for the Partnership for Prescription Assistance (PPA), Williams is also active with the nonprofit MS Foundation, which he founded after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 1999.
[d01s002] Williams is also noted for his service in both the Marine Corps and the Navy, from which he was honorably discharged after 15 years of service.

[d04p000] Ray Stevens
[d04s000] Harold Ray Ragsdale (born January 24, 1939), known professionally as Ray Stevens, is an American country and pop singer-songwriter and comedian, known for his Grammy-winning recordings "Everything Is Beautiful" and "Misty", as well as comedic hits such as "Gitarzan" and "The Streak".
[d04s001] He has worked as a producer, music arranger, songwriter, television host, and solo artist; been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, the Georgia Music Hall of Fame, and the Christian Music Hall of Fame; and received Gold Albums for his music sales.

[d09p003] Donald C. Paup
[d09s003] Paup played on all U.S. Thomas Cup teams between 1963 and 1973.
[d09s004] He was elected to the U.S. Badminton Hall of Fame, now called the Walk of Fame, in 1973.

[d05p000] Salomon Brothers
[d05s000] Salomon Brothers was a Wall Street investment bank, known as a bulge bracket company.
[d05s001] Founded in 1910 by three brothers (Arthur, Herbert and Percy) along with a clerk named Ben Levy, it remained a partnership until the early 1980s, when it was acquired by the commodity trading firm Phibro Corporation and became "Salomon Inc." Eventually, Salomon (NYSE:SB) was acquired by Travelers Group in 1998; and, following the latter's merger with Citicorp that same year, Salomon became part of Citigroup.
[d05s002] Although the Salomon name carried on as Salomon Smith Barney, which were the investment banking operations of Citigroup, the name was abandoned in October 2003 after a series of financial scandals that tarnished the bank's reputation.

[d03p000] Lysin
[d03s000] Lysins, also known as endolysins or murein hydrolases, are hydrolytic enzymes produced by bacteriophages in order to cleave the host's cell wall during the final stage of the lytic cycle.
[d03s001] Lysins are highly evolved enzymes that are able to target one of the five bonds in peptidoglycan (murein), the main component of bacterial cell walls, which allows the release of progeny virions from the lysed cell.
[d03s002] Cell-wall-containing Archaea are also lysed by specialized pseudomurein-cleaving lysins, while most archaeal viruses employ alternate mechanisms.

[d08p000] Fremont High School (Oakland, California)
[d08s000] Fremont High School is an urban public high school located in the Fruitvale District of East Oakland, California, United States.
[d08s001] It was formerly a group of smaller high schools located on the same campus and known as Fremont Federation of High Schools.
[d08s002] The school's present configuration is that of the "wall to wall" career academies model, consisting of a 9th Grade House which feeds into one of three California Partnership Academies (CPA), specifically the Architecture Academy, Mandela Law & Public Service Academy, and Media Academy.

[d00p000] Orthodox Jewish feminism
[d00s000] Orthodox Jewish feminism (also known as Orthodox feminism amongst Jews) is a movement in Orthodox Judaism which seeks to further the cause of a more egalitarian approach to Jewish practice within the bounds of Jewish Law.
[d00s001] The major organizations of this movement is the Jewish Orthodox Feminist Alliance (JOFA) in North America, and Women of the Wall (WOW) and its affiliates in Israel and internationally, known as ICWOW - The International Committee for Women of the Wall.
[d00s002] In Israel, the leading Orthodox feminist organization is Kolech (http://www.kolech.org.il), started by Dr. Hannah Kehat.

[d09p000] Donald C. Paup
[d09s000] Donald Clark Paup (April 2, 1939 – August 7, 2012) was an American badminton player who won national and international titles from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s.
[d09s001] Primarily a doubles specialist, he was known for his quick racket and tactical astuteness.
[d09s002] He was ranked first in the U.S. men's doubles for twelve consecutive seasons (1965–1976); all but the last of these in a partnership with fellow left-hander Jim Poole that was consistently competitive at the world class level.

context:
[d06p000] Glaramara
[d06s000] Glaramara is a fell in the English Lake District in Cumbria.
[d06s001] It is a substantial fell that is part of a long ridge that stretches for over six kilometres from Stonethwaite in Borrowdale up to the important mountain pass of Esk Hause.
[d06s002] The summit of Glaramara at 783 m (2,569 ft) is the central point of this ridge, which separates the valleys of Langstrath and Grains Gill.

[d04p000] Stonethwaite
[d04s000] Stonethwaite is a small village in the Lake District in the English county of Cumbria.
[d04s001] Historically part of Cumberland, it is situated in the valley of the Stonethwaite Beck, a side valley of Borrowdale, and within the Lake District National Park.
[d04s002] It is on the Cumbria Way long distance footpath.

[d01p000] Borrowdale
[d01s000] Borrowdale is a valley and civil parish in the English Lake District in the Borough of Allerdale in Cumbria, England.

[d09p000] Eagle Crag
[d09s000] Eagle Crag is a fell in the Lake District in Cumbria, England, it is situated near the village of Stonethwaite where the valleys of Langstrath and Greenup join.
[d09s001] Impressive walls of crag look down upon Stonethwaite, making Eagle Crag the most arresting sight from that settlement.
[d09s002] It can be climbed direct by the average walker, picking a route between the rock faces.

question: Who passed away first Robert Graves or Dino Buzzati ?
context:
[d07p000] Robert Graves
[d07s000] Robert von Ranke Graves (24 July 1895 – 7 December 1985), also known as Robert Ranke Graves and most commonly Robert Graves, was an English poet, novelist, critic and classicist.
[d07s001] In a way similar to Oscar Wilde, Robert Graves was a Celticist and student of Irish mythology, by the influence of his father Alfred Perceval Graves, a celebrated Irish poet — with William Wilde, these families were inheritors of the Gaelic revival.
[d07s002] He produced more than 140 works.

[d05p000] The Seven Messengers
[d05s000] The Seven Messengers (Italian: I sette messaggeri ) is a collection of short stories written by Dino Buzzati and published as a book in 1942.
[d05s001] It contains nineteen short tales, in which the characters often interact with the presence of the fantastic and/or death, many of which are left unconcluded, leaving the reader in suspense or trying to guess their ending.
[d05s002] "The Seven Messengers" is also the name of the book's first short story.

[d06p000] Bàrnabo delle montagne
[d06s000] Bàrnabo delle montagne ("Bàrnabo of the mountains") is a 1933 novel by the Italian writer Dino Buzzati.
[d06s001] It tells the story of a young forest ranger who belongs to a community which guards a storage with explosives, but is expelled after running away during a robber attack.
[d06s002] The book was the basis for the 1994 film "Barnabo of the Mountains", directed by Mario Brenta.

[d00p000] Larger than Life (novel)
[d00s000] Larger than Life (Italian: Il grande ritratto ) is a 1960 novel by the Italian writer Dino Buzzati.
[d00s001] It tells the story of a scientist who becomes entangled with a large electronic machine in which the woman he loves is reincarnated.
[d00s002] The book is considered to be the first serious novel of Italian science fiction, with content that goes beyond light entertainment.

[d04p000] Il segreto del Bosco Vecchio
[d04s000] Il segreto del Bosco Vecchio ("the secret of the Old Woods") is a 1935 novel by the Italian writer Dino Buzzati.
[d04s001] It tells the story of a general who is about to cut down an old forest for the sake of financial gain, but discovers that the forest is inhabited by invisible spirits.
[d04s002] Buzzati wrote the novel with inspiration from Arthur Rackham's illustrations for fairy tales and fables.

[d03p000] Sessanta racconti
[d03s000] Sessanta racconti ("sixty stories") is a 1958 short story collection by the Italian writer Dino Buzzati.
[d03s001] The first 36 stories had been published previously, while the rest were new.
[d03s002] Subjects covered include the horror and surreality of life in a modern city, the existential aspects of advanced technology, metaphysical ideas as well as fantasy realms.

[d09p000] Dino Buzzati
[d09s000] Dino Buzzati-Traverso (] ; 14 October 1906 – 28 January 1972) was an Italian novelist, short story writer, painter and poet, as well as a journalist for "Corriere della Sera".
[d09s001] His worldwide fame is mostly due to his novel "The Tartar Steppe", but he is also known for his well received collections of short stories.

[d08p006] Joanna Wajs
[d08s006] She translates from Italian into Polish, including works by Oriana Fallaci, Dino Buzzati, Gian Antonio Stella and Valerio Evangelisti.
[d08s007] She is also the editor of a column on poetry for the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza.

[d01p000] Barnabo of the Mountains
[d01s000] Barnabo of the Mountains (Italian: "Barnabo delle montagne" ) is a 1994 Italian drama film directed by Mario Brenta.
[d01s001] It is based on Dino Buzzati's novel "Bàrnabo delle montagne".
[d01s002] It was entered into the 1994 Cannes Film Festival.

[d07p003] Robert Graves
[d07s003] Graves's poems—together with his translations and innovative analysis and interpretations of the Greek myths; his memoir of his early life, including his role in the First World War, "Good-Bye to All That"; and his speculative study of poetic inspiration, "The White Goddess"—have never been out of print.
[d07s004] Irish literature deeply affected Graves' White Goddess theories, specifically the genre aisling.

[d01s000] Thomas Fitch (January 27, 1838 – November 12, 1923) was an American lawyer and politician.
[d01s001] He defended President Brigham Young of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and other church leaders when Young and his denomination were prosecuted for polygamy in 1871 and 1872.
[d01s002] He also successfully defended Virgil, Morgan, and Wyatt Earp along with Doc Holliday when they were accused of murdering Billy Clanton, and Tom and Frank McLaury during the October 25, 1881 Gunfight at the O.K. Corral.

[d03p000] Doc Holliday

[d03s001] He is best known for his role as a temporary deputy marshal in the events leading up to and following the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral.

[d02p000] Hour of the Gun
[d02s000] Hour of the Gun is a 1967 Western film depicting Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday during their 1881 battles against Ike Clanton and his brothers in the Gunfight at the O.K. [d02s001] The movie was directed by John Sturges.

[d00p000] O.K. Corral hearing and aftermath
[d00s000] The O.K. Corral hearing and aftermath was the direct result of the 30-second Gunfight at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona Territory on October 26, 1881.
[d00s001] During that confrontation, Deputy U.S. Marshal and Tombstone Town Marshal Virgil Earp, Assistant Town Marshal Morgan Earp, and temporary deputy marshals Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday shot and killed Billy Clanton, and Tom and Frank McLaury.
[d00s002] Billy's brother Ike, who had repeatedly threatened to kill the Earps for some time, had been present at the gunfight but was unarmed and fled.

[d08p006] Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
[d08s006] Virgil, Morgan, and Doc Holliday were wounded, but Wyatt Earp was unharmed.
[d08s007] The shootout has come to represent a period of the American Old West when the frontier was virtually an open range for outlaws, largely unopposed by law enforcement officers who were spread thin over vast territories.

[d05p000] Morgan Earp
[d05s000] Morgan Seth Earp (April 24, 1851 – March 18, 1882) was a Tombstone, Arizona Special Policeman when he helped his brothers Virgil and Wyatt and Doc Holliday confront outlaw Cowboys in the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral on October 26, 1881.
[d05s001] All three Earp brothers had been the target of repeated death threats made by the Cowboys who were upset by the Earps' interference in their illegal activities.
[d05s002] The lawmen killed Cowboys Tom and Frank McLaury and Billy Clanton.

[d07p000] Virgil Earp
[d07s000] Virgil Walter Earp (July 18, 1843 – October 19, 1905) was both deputy U.S. marshal and Tombstone, Arizona City Marshal when he led his brothers Morgan and Wyatt and Doc Holliday in a confrontation with outlaw Cowboys at the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral on October 26, 1881.

[d08s004] Billy Clanton and both McLaury brothers were killed.
[d08s005] Ike Clanton claimed that he was unarmed and ran from the fight, along with Billy Claiborne.

[d07p003] Virgil Earp
[d07s003] All four lawmen were charged with murder by Ike Clanton, who had run from the gunfight.
[d07s004] During a month-long preliminary hearing, Judge Wells Spicer exonerated the men, concluding they had been performing their duty.

[d01p006] Cell fate determination
[d01s006] This is one of the reasons that model systems such as the fly ("Drosophila melanogaster"), the mouse (Muridae), and the leech ("Helobdella"), can all be used to study embryogenesis and developmental biology relevant to other animals, including humans.
[d01s007] What continues to be discovered and investigated is how the basic set of proteins (and mRNAs) are expressed differentially between cells types, temporally and spatially; and whether this is responsible for the vast diversity of organisms produced.
[d01s008] This leads to one of the key questions of developmental biology of how is cell fate determined.

[d06p000] Retinoblastoma protein
[d06s000] The retinoblastoma protein (protein name abbreviated pRb; gene name abbreviated RB or RB1) is a tumor suppressor protein that is dysfunctional in several major cancers.
[d06s001] One function of pRb is to prevent excessive cell growth by inhibiting cell cycle progression until a cell is ready to divide.
[d06s002] When the cell is ready to divide, pRb is phosphorylated, becomes inactive and allows cell cycle progression.

[d02s001] He is the lead vocalist and sole member of the act, using a backup band while on tour.

question: Are Power Grid and Vanished Planet both cooperative board games?
context:
[d00p000] Vanished Planet
[d00s000] Vanished Planet is a cooperative board game that debuted at the World Boardgaming Championships in 2003.
[d00s001] "Vanished Planet" pits the players against a time limit; the players must succeed in a certain number of goals before this time limit is reached, or they all lose.

[d05p003] Pandemic (board game)
[d05s003] The game is unlike most board games in that the gameplay is cooperative, rather than competitive.
[d05s004] Through the combined effort of all the players, the goal is to discover all four cures before any of several game-losing conditions are reached.

[d08p000] Power Grid
[d08s000] Power Grid is the English-language edition of the multiplayer German-style board game Funkenschlag (in its second incarnation) designed by Friedemann Friese and first published in 2004.
[d08s001] Power Grid is published by Rio Grande Games.

[d05p000] Pandemic (board game)
[d05s000] Pandemic is a cooperative board game designed by Matt Leacock and published by Z-Man Games in 2007.
[d05s001] "Pandemic" is based on the premise that four diseases have broken out in the world, each threatening to wipe out a region.
[d05s002] The game accommodates 2 to 4 players, each playing one of five possible specialists: dispatcher, medic, scientist, researcher, or operations expert.

[d03p000] Power Grid Company of Bangladesh
[d03s000] Power Grid Company of Bangladesh is the sole electric power transmission organization in Bangladesh.
[d03s001] It is a government company that owns and operates the power grid in Bangladesh.
[d03s002] It is a subsidiary of Power Development Board.

[d02p003] National Grid Corporation of the Philippines
[d02s003] As a common carrier, it must provide non-discriminatory access to its transmission system.
[d02s004] It is subject to the standards set by the Philippine Grid Code and the Transmission Development Plan.
[d02s005] It also updates the daily power situation outlook for Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao by determining the available capacity, system peak, and gross reserve (all of which are in units of MW or megawatts).

[d06p009] Neuhof Substation
[d06s009] In April 1990 the plant was shut down and between 2003 and 2005 the machines were dismantled.
[d06s010] The machine halls stand still today and are used by Harzenergie for internal purposes.

[d04p003] Advanced Distribution Automation
[d04s003] Electric power transmission systems typically operate above 110kV, whereas Electricity distribution systems operate at lower voltages.
[d04s004] Normally, electric utilities with SCADA systems have extensive control over transmission-level equipment, and increasing control over distribution-level equipment via distribution automation.
[d04s005] However, they often are unable to control smaller entities such as Distributed energy resources (DERs), buildings, and homes.

[d02p000] National Grid Corporation of the Philippines
[d02s000] The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is a private company that was created on January 15, 2009 through RA 9511.
[d02s001] It is a consortium of 3 corporations, namely Monte Oro Grid Resources Corporation, Calaca High Power Corporation, and the State Grid Corporation of China.
[d02s002] As the franchise holder, it is in charge of operating, managing, maintaining, and expanding the country's Philippine government or state-owned (through National Transmission Corporation or TransCo) power grid, controls the supply and demand of power by determining the power mix through the selection of power plants to put online (i.e., to signal power plants to produce power, as power plants will only produce power or feed their power to the transmission grid when directed by NGCP).

[d06p003] Neuhof Substation
[d06s003] Through the Neuhof substation up to 40 MVA could be imported.
[d06s004] Up to 25 MVA of the imported power could be fed via 5 rotary motor-generators, which were manufactured by Siemens and used for the compensation of frequency fluctuations of the East German power grid, into the power grid of West Germany.
[d06s005] Additionally power was fed directly from the East German power grid into the grids of Bad Sachsa, Walkenried, Zorge and Wieda.

question: Were both Alvin Lee and Chad Gray lead vocalists for bands?
context:
[d04p000] Chad Gray
[d04s000] Chad Gray (born October 16, 1971), is the lead vocalist for the groove metal supergroup Hellyeah and former lead vocalist for American heavy metal band Mudvayne.

[d00p000] Beautiful Monsters Tour
[d00s000] The Beautiful Monsters Tour was a North American concert tour co-headlined by American rock bands Hole and Marilyn Manson.
[d00s001] Launched in support of each band's respective third full-length studio LPs, 1998's "Celebrity Skin" and "Mechanical Animals", the tour was planned to run from February 28, 1999 until April 27, with 37 shows confirmed.
[d00s002] However, due to a highly publicized altercation between the bands' respective lead vocalists, the tour only visited arenas until March 14, for a total of 9 shows before Hole withdrew from the bill.

[d02p000] Alvin Lee
[d02s000] Alvin Lee (born Graham Anthony Barnes; 19 December 1944 – 6 March 2013) was an English singer and guitarist, best known as the lead vocalist and lead guitarist of the blues rock band Ten Years After.

[d03p000] Wheeler End Studios
[d03s000] Wheeler End Studios is Alvin Lee's former recording studio until recently leased to Oasis.
[d03s001] Oasis recorded several of their later albums there as well as other musicians, including George Harrison, Paul Weller, Robbie Williams, Proud Mary, The Stereophonics, and Emily All Over, a local band based in High Wycombe.
[d03s002] The Engineer for many of these bands was Stuart Epps.

[d07p000] Hellyeah
[d07s000] Hellyeah is an American heavy metal supergroup, consisting of Mudvayne vocalist Chad Gray, former Nothingface guitarist Tom Maxwell, bass player Kyle Sanders, guitarist Christian Brady and former Pantera and Damageplan drummer Vinnie Paul.
[d07s001] The idea to form a supergroup originated in 2000 on the Tattoo the Earth tour, although plans were constantly put on hold due to scheduling conflicts.
[d07s002] The summer of 2006 allowed the band to take the project seriously and record its first album.

[d09p003] Miracle (Nonpoint album)
[d09s003] The album was recorded in Racine, WI and was produced by Mudvayne singer Chad Gray and guitarist Greg Tribbett.

[d06p003] By the People, for the People
[d06s003] If the album was pre-ordered through the Sony Music Store, it was packaged with a free lithograph of the lyrics to "Dull Boy", signed and numbered by Mudvayne vocalist Chad Gray.
[d06s004] If it was ordered after the disc was released, the lithograph was shipped approximately three weeks later and was neither signed nor numbered.

[d08p000] In Tennessee
[d08s000] Alvin Lee In Tennessee is a studio album by Alvin Lee released in 2004.

[d05p000] So Sad
[d05s000] "So Sad" is a song by English musician George Harrison that was released on his 1974 album "Dark Horse".
[d05s001] Harrison originally recorded the song for his previous album, "Living in the Material World", before giving it to Alvin Lee, the guitarist and singer with Ten Years After.
[d05s002] Lee recorded it – as "So Sad (No Love of His Own)" – with gospel singer Mylon LeFevre for their 1973 album "On the Road to Freedom".

[d06p000] By the People, for the People
[d06s000] By the People, for the People is a compilation album by American heavy metal band Mudvayne.
[d06s001] It was released on November 27, 2007 by Epic Records.
[d06s002] The album features a track listing chosen entirely by the band's fans, with the band determining which version appears on the record (e.g. live, demo, acoustic), as well as two new songs, "Dull Boy" and a cover of The Police's song "King of Pain" (both produced by Dave Fortman).

context:
[d05p000] No. 1455 Flight RAF
[d05s000] No. 1455 (Fighter) Flight was formed at RAF Tangmere, West Sussex on 7 July 1941, equipped with Turbinlite Douglas Boston and Douglas Havoc aircraft.
[d05s001] On operations they co-operated with the Hawker Hurricanes of 1 Squadron and 3 Squadron.
[d05s002] The flight was replaced with 534 Squadron on 2 September 1942.

[d08p000] Hawker Hurricane
[d08s000] The Hawker Hurricane is a British single-seat fighter aircraft of the 1930s–1940s that was designed and predominantly built by Hawker Aircraft Ltd for the Royal Air Force (RAF).
[d08s001] Although overshadowed by the Supermarine Spitfire, the aircraft became renowned during the Battle of Britain, accounting for 60 percent of the RAF air victories in the battle, and served in all the major theatres of the Second World War.

[d02p000] Hawker Typhoon
[d02s000] The Hawker Typhoon (Tiffy in RAF slang), is a British single-seat fighter-bomber, produced by Hawker Aircraft.
[d02s001] It was intended to be a medium–high altitude interceptor, as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane but several design problems were encountered and it never completely satisfied this requirement.

[d06p000] Hawker Tornado
[d06s000] The Hawker Tornado was a British single-seat fighter aircraft design of World War II for the Royal Air Force as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane.
[d06s001] The planned production of Tornados was cancelled after the engine it was designed to use—the Rolls-Royce Vulture—proved unreliable in service.
[d06s002] A parallel airframe with the Napier Sabre continued into production as the Hawker Typhoon.

context:
[d02p000] Tappi Tíkarrass
[d02s000] Tappi Tíkarrass was an Icelandic punk band which added elements of funk, rock and jazz to their music, marking a difference from other traditional bands at that time.
[d02s001] The band is also considered the first serious music project of now renowned singer Björk Guðmundsdóttir.

[d04p000] Nýtt líf
[d04s000] Nýtt Líf (   , English: "New Life") is an Icelandic film directed by Þráinn Bertelsson and released in 1983.
[d04s001] The film is a comedy shot in the Westman Islands and stars Eggert Þorleifsson and Karl Ágúst Úlfsson, among others.
[d04s002] The music features several musicians including the band Tappi Tíkarrass (of which Björk was a member), which contributed the songs "Sperglar" and "Kukl" (a.k.a. "Seiður").

[d00p000] Bitið fast í vitið
[d00s000] Bitið fast í vitið (roughly "Bite Hard In Your Mind" in Icelandic) is the début EP of Icelander punk/pop group Tappi Tíkarrass .
[d00s001] It was released in late-1982 on the Spor label, within a year of the band's formation in September 1981 – led by vocalists Björk and Eyþór Arnalds .
[d00s002] This was the band's most punk-oriented release and contains five tracks, featuring one in English, "London".

question: What comic book does Hershel Greene and Carl Grimes appear in as characters?
context:
[d04p003] Hershel Greene
[d04s003] In both the comics and television series, he is initially introduced saving the life of Carl Grimes, the son of Rick Grimes after he is shot by one of Hershel's neighbors, Otis, and becomes the moral center of the group .

[d02p000] Carl Grimes
[d02s000] Carl Grimes is a fictional character from the comic book series "The Walking Dead" and is portrayed by Chandler Riggs in the American television series of the same name, which airs on AMC in the United States.
[d02s001] The character was created by writer Robert Kirkman and artist Tony Moore, and debuted in "The Walking Dead" #2 in 2003.
[d02s002] In both forms of media, Carl is the son of primary protagonist Rick Grimes, and his wife Lori Grimes, and is one of the longest-surviving characters and one of the few original Atlanta survivors still alive.

[d06p000] Lori Grimes
[d06s000] Lori Grimes is a fictional character from the comic book series "The Walking Dead" and is portrayed by Sarah Wayne Callies in the American television series of the same name in the show's first three seasons.
[d06s001] Created by writer Robert Kirkman and artist Tony Moore, the character made her debut in "The Walking Dead" #2 in 2003.
[d06s002] In both forms of media, she is the wife of protagonist Rick Grimes and mother of Carl, and serves as the emotional core of the group.

[d00p000] Nebraska (The Walking Dead)
[d00s000] "Nebraska" is the eighth episode and mid-season premiere of the second season, and 14th episode overall of the post-apocalyptic horror television series "The Walking Dead".
[d00s001] It originally aired on AMC in the United States on February 12, 2012.
[d00s002] In the episode, the survivors deal with the aftermath of the barn shooting, which causes Hershel Greene (Scott Wilson) to order Rick's group to leave and then start drinking and disappear from the group, leading Rick Grimes (Andrew Lincoln) and Glenn (Steven Yeun) to try to find him.

[d05p003] Pretty Much Dead Already
[d05s003] Hershel Greene (Scott Wilson) sets a deadline for the group to leave, unless Rick Grimes (Andrew Lincoln) does a difficult task.
[d05s004] Meanwhile, Shane Walsh (Jon Bernthal) slowly loses his sanity after many secrets around him are revealed and Carol Peletier begins to question whether her daughter, Sophia will be found.

[d03p000] Rosita Espinosa
[d03s000] Rosita Espinosa is a fictional character from the comic book series "The Walking Dead" and is portrayed by Christian Serratos in the American television series of the same name.
[d03s001] She accompanies Eugene Porter and Abraham Ford on a mission to Washington, D.C. In the comic book series, she joins Rick Grimes' group after they leave Hershel Greene's farm and go to DC.
[d03s002] Eventually Eugene is revealed to have lied but they continue onto Washington anyway, since he was still convinced the city would offer greater chance of survival, and they eventually find the Alexandria Safe-Zone.

[d09p000] Beth Greene
[d09s000] Beth Greene is a fictional character from the American horror drama television series "The Walking Dead", created by season two showrunner Glen Mazzara, and portrayed by Emily Kinney.
[d09s001] Daughter of veterinarian and farmer Hershel Greene, and younger, half-sister of Maggie, the character has no counterpart in the comic book series on which the show is based.

[d01p000] Sophia Peletier
[d01s000] Sophia Peletier is a fictional character from the comic series "The Walking Dead" and is portrayed by Madison Lintz in the television series of the same name.
[d01s001] She is the daughter of Carol Peletier, who is fiercely protective of her, as is Carl Grimes, with whom she becomes close friends during the zombie outbreak.
[d01s002] She becomes a major focal point in both media, despite her limited involvement in many of the central conflicts faced by the other characters.

[d04p000] Hershel Greene
[d04s000] Hershel Greene is a fictional character in "The Walking Dead" whose role is depicted in the comic book, television series as portrayed by Scott Wilson and the game series.
[d04s001] He is the widowed owner of a farm in Georgia and has previous experience in the veterinary fields.
[d04s002] A devout Christian, with uncompromising morals and a stubborn attitude, Hershel remains fiercely protective of his large family, despite his many losses.

[d06p003] Lori Grimes
[d06s003] The character escaped the zombie apocalypse with Carl and Rick's partner Shane Walsh, and, believing her husband to be dead, started a relationship with Shane.

question: Were both the Battle of Stones River and the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River fought in the 19th century?
context:
[d04p000] Battle of Stones River
[d04s000] The Battle of Stones River or Second Battle of Murfreesboro, was fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863, in Middle Tennessee, as the culmination of the Stones River Campaign in the Western Theater of the American Civil War.
[d04s001] Of the major battles of the Civil War, Stones River had the highest percentage of casualties on both sides.
[d04s002] Although the battle itself was inconclusive, the Union Army's repulse of two Confederate attacks and the subsequent Confederate withdrawal were a much-needed boost to Union morale after the defeat at the Battle of Fredericksburg, and it dashed Confederate aspirations for control of Middle Tennessee.

[d06p000] Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River
[d06s000] The Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River, also known as the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on () or the Second Phase Campaign Western Sector (), was a decisive battle in the Korean War, and it took place from November 25 to December 2, 1950, along the Ch'ongch'on River Valley in the northwestern part of North Korea.
[d06s001] In response to the successful Chinese First Phase Campaign against the United Nations forces, General Douglas MacArthur launched the Home-by-Christmas Offensive to evict the Chinese forces from Korea and to end the war.
[d06s002] Anticipating this reaction, the Chinese People's Volunteer Army Commander Peng Dehuai planned a counteroffensive, dubbed the "Second Phase Campaign", against the advancing UN forces.

[d05p000] Joseph L. Follett
[d05s000] Joseph Leonard Follett (February 16, 1843 – April 1, 1907) was an American soldier who fought in the American Civil War.
[d05s001] Follett received the country's highest award for bravery during combat, the Medal of Honor, for his action during the Battle of Island Number Ten in New Madrid, Missouri on 3 March 1862 and the Battle of Stones River in Tennessee on 31 December 1862.
[d05s002] He was honored with the award on 19 September 1890.

[d00p000] Battle of Glendale (Skye)
[d00s000] The Battle of Glendale was a battle fought on the Inner Hebridean island of Skye, between the MacDonalds of Sleat and the MacDonalds of Clanranald, against the MacLeods of Harris and Dunvegan and the MacLeods of Lewis.
[d00s001] According to MacLeod tradition preserved in the early 19th century, the battle was fought in about the year 1490; yet it has been recently suggested that the battle more likely took place sometime after 1513.
[d00s002] MacLeod tradition records that the battle was the 'most tremendous battle' that the clan ever fought—although the clan was victorious, it never fully recovered from its severe losses.

[d01p003] Battle of Berestechko
[d01s003] The Polish camp was on the river opposite Berestechko and faced south, towards the Cossack army about two kilometers away, whose right flank was against the River Pliashivka (Pliashova) and the Tatar army on their left flank.
[d01s004] It was probably the largest European land battle of the 17th century.

[d00p003] Battle of Glendale (Skye)
[d00s003] MacLeod tradition relates how the MacDonalds originally had the upper hand during the conflict, but when the MacLeod's sacred Fairy Flag was unfurled the MacLeods gained heart and won the battle.

[d07p003] Savage's Station, Virginia
[d07s003] The house served as the nucleus of a large field hospital during and after the battle of Seven Pines and the Seven Days Battles.
[d07s004] The house also functioned as General George B. McClellan's headquarters during the battle of Savage's Station on June 29, 1862.
[d07s005] Although the house survived the battle in 1862, it was burned by Federal cavalry under General Philip H. Sheridan in 1864.

[d03p003] Umba River (Tanzania)
[d03s003] Just before the Umba flows into the Indian Ocean, it crosses the border to Kenya.
[d03s004] The mouth itself marks the most eastern point on the border between Tanzania and Kenya, which was largely made in a straight line to the northwest towards Lake Victoria in the 19th Century.
[d03s005] On the upper reaches of the river in the mid-1960s rich deposits of precious stones, including sapphires and Spessartine, were discovered.

[d08p003] Collins Ferry Historic District
[d08s003] The Collins Farm includes 19th century farm outbuildings, the family cemetery, a mill site along the river, and the site where stones for the mill's construction and grinding stones were quarried.
[d08s004] The Hubbard Farm is located south and east of the Collins Farm, and is accessed via a private drive that forms part of the historic road leading to Collins Ferry.
[d08s005] Hubbard Farm includes a Greek Revival farmhouse built in 1856, and also includes 19th century outbuildings, a family cemetery, and the remains of a slave quarters.

[d01p000] Battle of Berestechko
[d01s000] The Battle of Berestechko (Polish: "Bitwa pod Beresteczkiem" ; Ukrainian: Берестецька битва, Битва під Берестечком ) was fought between the Ukrainian Cossacks, led by Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky, aided by their Crimean Tatar allies, and a Polish army under King John II Casimir.
[d01s001] It was a battle of a Cossack rebellion in Ukraine that took place in the years 1648–1657 after the expiration of a two-year truce.
[d01s002] Fought from 28 to 30 June 1651, the battle took place in the province of Volhynia, on the hilly plain south of the Styr River.

[d05p000] No. 1455 Flight RAF

[d08p000] Hawker Hurricane
[d08s000] The Hawker Hurricane is a British single-seat fighter aircraft of the 1930s–1940s that was designed and predominantly built by Hawker Aircraft Ltd for the Royal Air Force (RAF).

[d02p000] Hawker Typhoon
[d02s000] The Hawker Typhoon (Tiffy in RAF slang), is a British single-seat fighter-bomber, produced by Hawker Aircraft.
[d02s001] It was intended to be a medium–high altitude interceptor, as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane but several design problems were encountered and it never completely satisfied this requirement.

[d06p000] Hawker Tornado
[d06s000] The Hawker Tornado was a British single-seat fighter aircraft design of World War II for the Royal Air Force as a replacement for the Hawker Hurricane.
[d06s001] The planned production of Tornados was cancelled after the engine it was designed to use—the Rolls-Royce Vulture—proved unreliable in service.
[d06s002] A parallel airframe with the Napier Sabre continued into production as the Hawker Typhoon.

question: Were both the Battle of Stones River and the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River fought in the 19th century?
context:
[d06p000] Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River
[d06s000] The Battle of the Ch'ongch'on River, also known as the Battle of the Ch'ongch'on () or the Second Phase Campaign Western Sector (), was a decisive battle in the Korean War, and it took place from November 25 to December 2, 1950, along the Ch'ongch'on River Valley in the northwestern part of North Korea.
[d06s001] In response to the successful Chinese First Phase Campaign against the United Nations forces, General Douglas MacArthur launched the Home-by-Christmas Offensive to evict the Chinese forces from Korea and to end the war.
[d06s002] Anticipating this reaction, the Chinese People's Volunteer Army Commander Peng Dehuai planned a counteroffensive, dubbed the "Second Phase Campaign", against the advancing UN forces.

[d04p000] Battle of Stones River
[d04s000] The Battle of Stones River or Second Battle of Murfreesboro, was fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863, in Middle Tennessee, as the culmination of the Stones River Campaign in the Western Theater of the American Civil War.
[d04s001] Of the major battles of the Civil War, Stones River had the highest percentage of casualties on both sides.
[d04s002] Although the battle itself was inconclusive, the Union Army's repulse of two Confederate attacks and the subsequent Confederate withdrawal were a much-needed boost to Union morale after the defeat at the Battle of Fredericksburg, and it dashed Confederate aspirations for control of Middle Tennessee.

[d03p003] Umba River (Tanzania)
[d03s003] Just before the Umba flows into the Indian Ocean, it crosses the border to Kenya.
[d03s004] The mouth itself marks the most eastern point on the border between Tanzania and Kenya, which was largely made in a straight line to the northwest towards Lake Victoria in the 19th Century.
[d03s005] On the upper reaches of the river in the mid-1960s rich deposits of precious stones, including sapphires and Spessartine, were discovered.

[d08p003] Collins Ferry Historic District
[d08s003] The Collins Farm includes 19th century farm outbuildings, the family cemetery, a mill site along the river, and the site where stones for the mill's construction and grinding stones were quarried.
[d08s004] The Hubbard Farm is located south and east of the Collins Farm, and is accessed via a private drive that forms part of the historic road leading to Collins Ferry.
[d08s005] Hubbard Farm includes a Greek Revival farmhouse built in 1856, and also includes 19th century outbuildings, a family cemetery, and the remains of a slave quarters.

[d00p000] Battle of Glendale (Skye)
[d00s000] The Battle of Glendale was a battle fought on the Inner Hebridean island of Skye, between the MacDonalds of Sleat and the MacDonalds of Clanranald, against the MacLeods of Harris and Dunvegan and the MacLeods of Lewis.
[d00s001] According to MacLeod tradition preserved in the early 19th century, the battle was fought in about the year 1490; yet it has been recently suggested that the battle more likely took place sometime after 1513.
[d00s002] MacLeod tradition records that the battle was the 'most tremendous battle' that the clan ever fought—although the clan was victorious, it never fully recovered from its severe losses.

[d05p000] Joseph L. Follett
[d05s000] Joseph Leonard Follett (February 16, 1843 – April 1, 1907) was an American soldier who fought in the American Civil War.
[d05s001] Follett received the country's highest award for bravery during combat, the Medal of Honor, for his action during the Battle of Island Number Ten in New Madrid, Missouri on 3 March 1862 and the Battle of Stones River in Tennessee on 31 December 1862.
[d05s002] He was honored with the award on 19 September 1890.

[d02p000] Register Cliff
[d02s000] Register Cliff is a sandstone cliff and featured key navigational landmark prominently listed in the 19th century guidebooks about the Oregon Trail, and a place where many emigrants chiseled the names of their families on the soft stones of the cliff it was one of the key checkpoint landmarks for parties heading west along the Platte River valley west of Fort John, Wyoming which allowed travelers to verify they were on the correct path up to South Pass and not moving into impassable mountain terrainsgeographically, it is on the eastern ascent of the Continental divide leading upward out of the great plains in the east of the U.S. state of Wyoming.
[d02s001] It is notable as a historic landmark for 'registering' hundreds of emigrants on the Oregon Trail (thus also the other northern Emigrant Trails that split off farther west such as the California Trail and Mormon Trail) who came to follow custom and inscribed their names on its rocks during the western migrations of the 19th century.
[d02s002] An estimated 500,000 emigrants used these trails from 1843–1869, with up to one-tenth dying along the way, usually due to disease.

[d01p000] Battle of Berestechko
[d01s000] The Battle of Berestechko (Polish: "Bitwa pod Beresteczkiem" ; Ukrainian: Берестецька битва, Битва під Берестечком ) was fought between the Ukrainian Cossacks, led by Hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky, aided by their Crimean Tatar allies, and a Polish army under King John II Casimir.
[d01s001] It was a battle of a Cossack rebellion in Ukraine that took place in the years 1648–1657 after the expiration of a two-year truce.
[d01s002] Fought from 28 to 30 June 1651, the battle took place in the province of Volhynia, on the hilly plain south of the Styr River.

question: Who lived longer Ellen Glasgow or N. Scott Momaday ?
context:
[d05p000] Ellen Glasgow
[d05s000] Ellen Anderson Gholson Glasgow (April 22, 1873 – November 21, 1945) was an American novelist who portrayed the changing world of the contemporary South.

[d07p003] Virginia (novel)
[d07s003] Today, "Virginia" is seen by many as an outstanding achievement in Glasgow's career, exactly because the author defied literary convention by questioning the foundations of American society around the dawn of the 20th century, be it capitalism, religion or racism.

[d04p000] Ellen Glasgow House
[d04s000] The Ellen Glasgow House, also known as the Branch-Glascow House, is a historic house at 1 West Main Street in Richmond, Virginia.
[d04s001] Built in 1841, it is nationally significant as the home of writer Ellen Glasgow (1873-1945) from 1887 until her death.
[d04s002] It was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1971.

[d06p000] The Shadowy Third and Other Stories
[d06s000] The Shadowy Third and Other Stories is a 1923 short story collection by Ellen Glasgow.
[d06s001] Glasgow published only this one short story collection during her lifetime, which included seven stories.
[d06s002] While Glasgow's novels receive more critical attention, scholarship on her stories continues into the twenty-first century.

[d02p000] N. Scott Momaday
[d02s000] Navarre Scott Momaday (born February 27, 1934) — known as N. Scott Momaday — is a Kiowa novelist, short story writer, essayist, and poet.
[d02s001] His novel "House Made of Dawn" was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1969, and is considered the first major work of the Native American Renaissance.
[d02s002] His follow-up work "The Way to Rainy Mountain" blended folklore with memoir.

[d01p000] The Way to Rainy Mountain
[d01s000] The Way to Rainy Mountain (1969) is a book by Pulitzer Prize winning author N. Scott Momaday.
[d01s001] It is about the journey of Momaday's Kiowa ancestors from their ancient beginnings in the Montana area to their final war and surrender to the United States Cavalry at Fort Sill, and subsequent resettlement near Rainy Mountain, Oklahoma.

[d03p000] House Made of Dawn
[d03s000] House Made of Dawn is a 1968 novel by N. Scott Momaday, widely credited as leading the way for the breakthrough of Native American literature into the mainstream.
[d03s001] It was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1969, and has also been noted for its significance in Native American Anthropology.

[d08p000] Robert Weil (editor)

[d00p000] Sheet music
[d00s000] Sheet music is a handwritten or printed form of music notation that uses modern musical symbols to indicate the pitches (melodies), rhythms or chords of a song or instrumental musical piece.

question: Who was an important leader of the Democratic-Republican Party?
context:
[d03p000] Albert Gallatin
[d03s000] Abraham Alfonse Albert Gallatin (January 29, 1761 – August 12, 1849) was a Swiss-American politician, diplomat, ethnologist and linguist.
[d03s001] He was an important leader of the Democratic-Republican Party, serving in various federal elective and appointed positions across four decades.
[d03s002] He represented Pennsylvania in the Senate and the House of Representatives before becoming the longest-tenured United States Secretary of the Treasury and serving as a high-ranking diplomat.

[d01p000] Democratic-Republican Party
[d01s000] The Democratic-Republican Party was an American political party formed by Thomas Jefferson and James Madison in 1791–93 to oppose the centralizing policies of the new Federalist Party run by Alexander Hamilton (1755/57-1804), who was secretary of the treasury and chief architect of George Washington's administration.
[d01s001] The new party controlled the presidency and Congress, as well as most states, from 1801 to 1825, during the First Party System.
[d01s002] It began in 1791 as one faction in Congress, and included many politicians who had been opposed to the new constitution.

[d02p009] Whig Party (United States)

[d02s010] The underlying political philosophy of the American Whig Party was not directly related to the British Whig party.

[d00p003] Presidency of Thomas Jefferson
[d00s003] After two terms, Jefferson was succeeded by Secretary of State James Madison, also of the Democratic-Republican Party.

[d09p000] Jeremiah Morrow
[d09s000] Jeremiah Morrow (October 6, 1771March 22, 1852) was a Democratic-Republican Party politician from Ohio.
[d09s001] He served as the ninth Governor of Ohio, and the last Democratic-Republican to do so.

[d00p000] Presidency of Thomas Jefferson
[d00s000] The presidency of Thomas Jefferson began on March 4, 1801, when he was inaugurated as the third President of the United States, and ended on March 4, 1809.
[d00s001] Jefferson assumed the office after defeating incumbent President John Adams in the 1800 presidential election.
[d00s002] The election was a realigning election in which the Democratic-Republican Party swept the Federalist Party out of power, ushering in a generation of Democratic-Republican dominance in American politics.

[d07p000] The Probability Broach
[d07s000] The Probability Broach is the 1979 first novel by American science fiction writer L. Neil Smith.
[d07s001] It is set in an alternate history, the so-called Gallatin Universe, where a libertarian society has formed on the North American continent, styled the North American Confederacy ("NAC").
[d07s002] This history was created when the Declaration of Independence has the word "unanimous" added to the preamble, to read that governments "derive their just power from the "unanimous" consent of the governed".

[d02p000] Whig Party (United States)
[d02s000] The Whig Party was a political party active in the middle of the 19th century in the United States.
[d02s001] Four US presidents belonged to the party while in office.
[d02s002] It emerged in the 1830s as the leading opponent of Jacksonians, pulling together former members of the National Republican (one of the successors of the Democratic-Republican Party) and Anti-Masonic Parties.

[d05p003] United States presidential election, 1800
[d05s003] The election was a realigning election that ushered in a generation of Democratic-Republican Party rule and the eventual demise of the Federalist Party in the First Party System.
[d05s004] It was a long, bitter re-match of the 1796 election between the pro-French and pro-decentralization Democratic-Republicans under Jefferson and Aaron Burr and the incumbent Adams and Charles Pinckney's pro-British and pro-centralization Federalists.
[d05s005] The chief political issues revolved around the fallout from the French Revolution, including opposition to the tax imposed by Congress to pay for the mobilization of the new army and the navy in the Quasi-War against France in 1798.

[d02p003] Whig Party (United States)
[d02s003] It had distant links to the upscale traditions of the Federalist Party.
[d02s004] Along with the rival Democratic Party, it was central to the Second Party System from the early 1840s to the mid-1860s.
[d02s005] It originally formed in opposition to the policies of President Andrew Jackson (in office 1829–37) and his Democratic Party.

context:
[d03p003] Ernst Abbe
[d03s003] He was a co-owner of Carl Zeiss AG, a German manufacturer of research microscopes, astronomical telescopes, planetariums and other optical systems.

[d07p000] Abbe error
[d07s000] Abbe error, named after Ernst Abbe, also called sine error, describes the magnification of angular error over distance.
[d07s001] For example, when one measures a point that is 1 meter away at 45 degrees, an angular error of 1 degree corresponds to a positional error of over 1.745 cm, equivalent to a distance-measurement error of 1.745%.

[d03p000] Ernst Abbe
[d03s000] Ernst Karl Abbe HonFRMS (23 January 1840 – 14 January 1905) was a German physicist, optical scientist, entrepreneur, and social reformer.
[d03s001] Together with Otto Schott and Carl Zeiss, he laid the foundation of modern optics.
[d03s002] Abbe developed numerous optical instruments.

[d00p000] Porro–Abbe prism
[d00s000] A Porro–Abbe prism (sometimes called a Abbe–Porro prism), named for Ignazio Porro and Ernst Abbe, is a type of reflection prism used in some optical instruments to alter the orientation of an image.
[d00s001] It is a variant of the more common double Porro prism configuration.

[d09p003] Othello error
[d09s003] The error is named after William Shakespeare's tragic play "Othello"; the dynamics between the two main characters, Othello and Desdemona are a particularly notable example of the error in practice.

[d06p000] Ernst-Abbe-Sportfeld
[d06s000] Ernst Abbe Sportfield is a sports facility in Jena, Germany.
[d06s001] It was dedicated on August 24, 1924 and was named after entrepreneur Ernst Abbe 15 years later.
[d06s002] The facility is in southern Jena, directly on the Saale River.

[d02p000] Description error
[d02s000] A description error or selection error is an error, or more specifically a human error, that occurs when a person performs the correct action on the wrong object due to insufficient specification of an action which would have led to a desired result.
[d02s001] This commonly happens when similar actions lead to different results.
[d02s002] A typical example is a panel with rows of identical switches, where it is easy to carry out a correct action (flip a switch) on a wrong switch due to their insufficient differentiation.

[d08p000] Bramble–Hilbert lemma
[d08s000] In mathematics, particularly numerical analysis, the Bramble–Hilbert lemma, named after James H. Bramble and Stephen Hilbert, bounds the error of an approximation of a function formula_1 by a polynomial of order at most formula_2 in terms of derivatives of formula_1 of order formula_4.
[d08s001] Both the error of the approximation and the derivatives of formula_1 are measured by formula_6 norms on a bounded domain in formula_7.
[d08s002] This is similar to classical numerical analysis, where, for example, the error of linear interpolation formula_1 can be bounded using the second derivative of formula_1.

[d05p000] Errors of impunity
[d05s000] Errors of impunity is a term used in Brian Forst's book "Errors of Justice" and in Robert Bohm's introduction to a special edition of "The Journal of Criminal Justice" on miscarriages of justice.
[d05s001] They are defined as lapses that result in criminals either remaining at large or receiving sanctions that are below a socially optimal level.
[d05s002] If convicting an innocent person, called a miscarriage of justice, is a Type I error for falsely identifying culpability (a "false positive"), then an error of impunity would be a Type II error of failing to find a culpable person guilty (a "false negative").

[d04p000] Van Abbemuseum
[d04s000] Van Abbemuseum (] ) is a museum of modern and contemporary art located in central Eindhoven, Netherlands, on the east bank of the Dommel river.
[d04s001] Established in 1936, the Abbe Museum is named after its founder, Henri van Abbe.
[d04s002] Van Abbe was a lover of modern art and wanted to enjoy it there from Eindhoven.

selected.title: Errors of impunity

facts.title: Errors of impunity
facts.text: Errors of impunity is a term used in Brian Forst's book "Errors of Justice" and in Robert Bohm's introduction to a special edition of "The Journal of Criminal Justice" on miscarriages of justice.

facts.title: Errors of impunity
facts.text: They are defined as lapses that result in criminals either remaining at large or receiving sanctions that are below a socially optimal level.

facts.title: Errors of impunity
facts.text: If convicting an innocent person, called a miscarriage of justice, is a Type I error for falsely identifying culpability (a "false positive"), then an error of impunity would be a Type II error of failing to find a culpable person guilty (a "false negative").

question: In the muti-sport games usually held every four years between nations around the Mediterranean Sea, Fatma Lanouar is best known for winning gold in which event?
context:
[d05p000] Fatma Lanouar
[d05s000] Fatma Lanouar (Arabic: فاطمة لأنور; born March 14, 1978) is a former female middle distance runner from Tunisia.

[d05s002] Lanouar set her personal best (4:06.91) in the 1,500 metres in 2000.

[d09s000] The Mediterranean Games are a multi-sport games held usually every four years, between nations around or very close to the Mediterranean Sea, where Europe, Africa, and Asia meet.

[d02s001] The Olympic Games are considered the world's foremost sports competition with more than 200 nations participating.
[d02s002] The Olympic Games are held every four years, with the Summer and Winter Games alternating by occurring every four years but two years apart.
